articles.text:
THE DOUBLE SHIFT SYSTEM.

IN accordance with our promise, we return to
Mr. TlA.RinsoN's article in the Fortnightly
Review. The writer agrees with Mr. BRASSEY
in his views on the "relay," or "double shift
system," and urges a variety of arguments to
prove that "the true solution of the difficulty
capital finds in utilizing its costly apparatus,"
(machinery) . appears to lie in the adoption of
this system.
The first question, however, to be solved in
relation to this proposal is its practicability.
On turning to Mr. BRA.ssEY's book it is observ-
able that scarcely any attempt to prove this
can be found, and in Mr. HARRISON'S article
the proof furnished rests altogether on as-
sumptions, which, until they are themselves
proved, are incapable of proving anything
else; as, for instance, when Mr. HARRISON
informs us that the body of workmen are not
a "fixed number," but rather an "eminently
elastic body," he by no means proves that they
could be increased up to nearly double their
number for the purpose of carrying out the plan
he advocates, andalle does not even hint how the
skill absolutely necessary is to be put into
their fingers so as to adapt them for the work
required.. We have had, it is true, "vast
reserves of surplus labour," and a "constant
stream of.emigration," but neither in England,

from which this is pouring out, nor in the
United States, of America, where it settles down
and rests, can it be turned to the uses pointed
out by Mr. IlinuisoN, for though a few weeks ,
of good feeding and right practice may turn a
farm labourer into a good "navvy," it will by
no means make him into an efficient artizan,
either in the manufacture of cotton, woollen,
linen, or silk.
It would be a loss of time to argue this
question on grounds other than these upon which
Mr. I3na.ssfw and Mr. 11A.,ll1tisoN ;have placed
it.; It is not meant to apply to agricultural
labour,', as there machinery may be said
scarcely to exist, and where it does there is no
kind of interference with its most economic
working. At harvest time, when bands are
scarce, the farmers will do all they can in this
way, but during the slack times—the bitter
winter months—to work machinery by relays
would be very unprofitable farming.
Then, again, in domestic trades, this sys-
tem could not be used to any extent beneficial
to the country, for reasons muoli the same as
those that apply to farming--,machines arc
not commonly employed, and where they are
the restrietions on their use cannot amount to
much. If ever the thought does enter into the
heads of any portion of our people to try the
relay system, its application must be in our
factories and great workshops, as it is in these
only where the short day is vehemently
inzisted on, or where capital can be said to

lie wastefully dormant whilst the machine
rests for the convenience of the human
worker.

Let us, therefore, for a moment confine
ourselves to. a consideration of the way in
which this double shift system would operate
in our great manufacturing districts. In
the first place, it may be observed that it
would be altogether out of the question
during periods of slack trade. Manufacturers
then voluntarily run short time; not having
sufficient outlets for what they produce, they
of themselves reduce the hours of labour, and
compel their workers for a good part of their
time to walk the streets, or sit at home in very
painful idleness. The power to overproduce
is the evil under such circumstances, and this
state of things is not brought about by any
designed tuition on the part of the employer or
the workman, and as no largo number of the
workers can take themselves away during a
period of this kind, pauperism increases, as
well as those other understood evils which
follow want of work in our manufacturing
districts. To talk of a " relay system" at
such a time as this would be as much out of
place as to preach tho virtue of abstinence to
people who can got nothing to oat. Frequently,
however, employment is good; that is, the
factories run full time and the masses of the
people are actively at work. What may be
called the ordinary condition of trade is that
state to which capital and labour in every
district acoominodate themselves. If the
existing machinery is slightly deficient it is
increased, find if hands are not sufficiently
abundant they are gradually drawn in from
outlying neighbourhoods. But, as a rule, in
all our manufacturing districts, and in all
branches of skilled, industry, there is in
ordinary times a fluctuating surplus of labour,
rather than a corresponding deficienoy.
But even under this condition of things the
"relay system" would not answer if it could
be used. Simply because when trade is in its
ordinary condition it could not bear 60 per
cont. being added to production, as no power
of increase, in home or foreign markets could
carry such an increase off, and the mere
plethora thus created would inevitably bring
paralysis.
If, however, we take things at their very
best, just as they' have been now for some
time back, how, we ask, could the " relay " or
"double shift system" be brought into use?
For some time now business of all sorts has
been more active than perhaps in the history
of England it was ever before known to be.
Not in one branch but in all branches. All
our factories have been working up to their
full power, and a very large number of new
factories have been built. Every available
" hand " has been sot to work, and many
unskilled persons have migrated into the
towns to take the places of partially skilled
persons who have been put upon work of a
more skilled kind than they had hitherto been
permitted to touch. Indeed, every effort has
been strained to get new labour into our
manufacturing districts, and perhaps with as
much success as over can be attained, so long
as the demand for such labour is a temporary,
not a permanent, condition of things.
Now, we ask any person disposed to
regard favourably the " double shift system "
—whether oven this almost unpreeedont,!d and
most unusual condition of trade could have
borne tho inorolised production of stioli a

system ?—whether the additional 60 per oent,
of production, thrown week after week into the
market, would not very soon have so increased
stooks as to make sales unprofitable? It must
not be forgotten that our tendency as a manu-
facturing population is to over production; and
our command of machinery, as a rule, enables
us to do this. Our " panics " catch us when
our manufacturers have been for some time
engaged in an active competitive race with
each other—when they have met each other
in the common markets of the world with too
much, with more than their customers could
conveniently take off their hands?
But suppose this was not the case, presuming
that over-abundant production was most
desirable under all circumstances, where, we
ask, are the " hands" to be got? If a busy
trade takes all, and has room for more, tbe
relays must be summoned from amongst the
ghosts of the dead factory-workers which troop
at night to the church-yards; though it is to
be feared that a summons to work again in the
factories would send them off in haste, faster
than the crowing of the morning cock.
We hesitate not to say that relays, never
wanted in slack or ordinary times, could never
be found in brisk times, and that, therefore,
the proposal on the face of it almost, is an im-
possibility which it would simply be a loss of
time to combat further. Mr. BDASSEY, in his
book, gives certain objections put forward by
Mr. ALEXANDER, which are merely senti-
mental. The real objection lies in the unwork-
able character of the plan, and beyond that
there is no use in going. The kind of work in
which Mr. BRASSEY'S firm was engaged (the
construction of railways, &c., esc.,) as an
exceptional industry, could, no doubt, resort to
such a system when pressed by necessity. Or a
few factories might adopt it; but for the
regular skilled industries of the country to
bring it into operation is truly out of the
question.
Before closing it may not be amiss to say,
that to adopt such a systein for the purpose of
making machinery more profitable, though,
perhaps, desirable under exceptional circum-
stances, is not quite a question of life and
death, so far as capital is concerned. Our
manufacturers have been doing very well;
they are not languishing and losing; they
are quite jolly in an accumulation of fat-
ness, and radiant over full coffers. Nobody
need grieve on their account, nor need any-
body plan for their welfare ; they can look the
whole world gaily in the face, and are as wide
awake as ever to turn every opportunity it
gives to golden account.
-Working men will have views of their own
on this subject. They know that such a
system would very soon degenerate into a six-
teen hour system for adult males not protected
by law, and, therefore, they would oppose it.
To our engineering industry it would be abso-
lutely ruinous, as it would practically add
60 per cent. to the amount of machinery at
work, and thus for years do away with all
demand for new machines. However, we have
already said, the thing is impossible, and
therefore may be safely left to those whose
interests it directly concerns.
In line, when there was any chance of
putting such a system into operation it would
not be required ; when required it would not
be practicable, and if practie4ble net asiralilel

give us, as its chief result, an unmanageable
overgrowth of pauperism, an appalling increase
in our "dangerous classes," in whose presence
even at the present moment our wisest and
most courageous statesmen tremble.

THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACTS.

TnE very able articles in your columns on
this most important subject have dealt with
the religious, moral, and social aspects of the
Acts; but I do not remember that any one
has yet pointed out, with proper effect, the
absurdity of hoping to stamp out the diseases
in question by dealing with one sex only. It
has been asserted repeatedly by the chief
supporters of the Contagious Disoi,es Acts,
and notably by the originators of the scheme
in this country, that women are the greatest
spreaders of disease; and that, in consequence,
women only require to be dealt with by the law
There are medical men who are sanguine
enough to hope that by means of one-sided
legislation these diseases may be stamped out;
but what would be said. of those persons who
attempted to stop the course of a river, by
damming up half the width of the stream?
to stamp out the cattle plague by killing the
cows only? to arrest small-pox by vaccinating
only girls? or to stamp out typhus or scarlet
fever, by sending girls to hospital, and per..
mitting infected boys to run about the streets?
Even supporters of the Contagious Diseases
Acts would regard such schemes as emanating
from the brain of a lunatic; they would cry
aloud concerning the folly or injustice of any
such attempt ; yet the country is called upon
to consider with favour the equally absurd
arrangements of the Contagious Diseases
Acts.

That these laws are utterly inexcusable and
useless as means for stamping out, or oven
materially lessening, the diseases of prostitu-
tion, so long as they fail to deal with men as
with women, can be proved by ample testi-
mony; and I propose, in the present article,
to cull that evidence from the writings, or
recorded evidence, of the most noted public
supporters of the Acts; indeed, they may be
called the fathers and nurses of the Acts.

Mr. BERKELY HILL is the honorary secre-

THE STRIKE AT MESSRS. CORBETT
AND M'CLYIYIONT'S.

--
The strike at Messrs. Corbett and M'ClYrnont's
at Brompton still continues, notwithstanding
strenuous efforts made by friends outside the trade
to bring about an amicable settlement. The only
concession that the firm are prepared to make is to
pay some of the leading men the 80. per hour,
and to take them back at once upon those terms.
Upon this being stated to the men it was at once
refused by those who would have been taken back
at those terms, who looked upon the offer as an
insult to the great body of their fellow workmen,
and as an attempt upon the part of the firm to
break up the unity and good feeling which havo
hitherto existed amongst the men. Meetings of
the men of the various trades were held on Satur-
day afternoon, at all of which resolutions Were
unanimously adopted to remain away from the
works until the firm consented to pay under the
terms of the new agreement, as they had already
done for one week.

waited on Messrs. Corbett and M' Cly rnont to prevail ,
on that firm to lower the wages and evade the
agreement as settled between the Central Associa- I
tion of Master Builders and the carpenters and
joiners, I beg to inform you that the Central
Association have had no communication whatever
with Messrs. Corbett and MsOlymont. The report
appearing in the newspapers to the effect that a
member of the committee of this association had
called upon Messrs. Corbett and lliPOlymont with
that objeut I find on inquiry to he equally untrue.
—.tours faithfully,
Mr. Charles Matkin.

STANLEY G. BIRD.

The first dividends to the carpenters, brick-
layers, painters, and plasterers on strike from
Messrs. Corbett and M'Clymont were paid on
Monday morning, the Carpenters' Committee
paying their men 15s. each, the Bricklayers and
Plasterers' Committee paying their men 12s. each,
the lahourers in their respective branches receiving
a proportionate share. The men expressed them-
selves quite satisfied with the result, with a deter-
mination not to resume work until their demands
were complied with. The unanimity displayed
by the men in coming out, and with which they
have acted while they have been on strike, is more
remarkable, as out of the 480 men who struck
work last Monday, not more than a were are
society men, and, therefore, could not be considered
=friable to any pressure from the union.

On Monday afternoon another open-air mass
Meeting was held on the vacant ground adjoining
St. Matthiaa's church, close to the northers
entrance to the Brompton Cemetery. Mr. Liel7,
(carpenter), who occupied the post of chairman,
was glad to be able to state that no one who came
out a week agli had shown the white feather ;
without any exception the Men on strike remained
true to each other, and if they only continued to
do so, the firm would ultimately concede their
just demand. Mr. Gook (Mason) proposed, and
Mr. Pearce (bricklayer) seconded, the following
resolution, viz.;—" That this meting of workmen
in each branch of the building trade resole to
continue the struggle until we obtain the same
terms as were paid to us, and" then withdrawn, hi
Messrs. Corbett and M'Clymont." Carried.

FRIDAY Mon...rm.—The position of the strike
remains without change. Neither side shows sul
signs of giving in, and idleness reigns sgonme
on the works of Messrs. Corbett and M'ClYmont,
On Tuesday SO= carpenters went in, but they 10
sooner went in than they "picked up" again, and
at a meeting held on Thursday morning the ranks
presented an unbroken front, although perhaps
not quite so crowded as heretofore,
as many of the
men in all the branches have succeeded in finding
work at full-priced shops and jobs.

articles.title: LONDON BAKERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON BAKERS.

Although it was generally believed that the dist*
puts in the Baking Trade was settled lag week it
was not so. On Monday the effects of the strike
became more generally knowii, and the proved 4

the movement could be more accurately estimated.
The struggle is conducted in different parts of the
metropolis with varying success, dependant ob-
viously on the wants and customs of the districts.
In the East and South gene:ally the operatives
have carried the day, and enlisted the sympathies
of their employers for the most part in the attain-
ment of their objects. In the centre and the
North there is a very general concession of the
demands which the yielding of one or two im-
portant firms who still stand out would render
universal; while on the other hand, at the West-
end there would seem to be a probability that
several of the largest employers will succeed in
their resistance to the operatives and be able to
maintain the old hours and terms. Mr. Spiking
and some of the other large firms in Belgravia,
Kensington, and Bayswater have, it is reported,
without difficulty supplied the places of the men
who have struck, and so greatly discouraged the
movement in the Western districts. It was re-
ported at the strike committee that fully three-
fourths of the gliniti trade of the metropolis was
virtually under the new system. The committee
in session throughout the day in Bartholomew-
close, where several meetings of the operatives
were hold, at all of which resolutions were car-
ried re-affirming the necessity of adhering to the
four to four system, and abolishing night-work.
'Workmen wore entreated by their fellows to
accept no other terms, however tempting, during
the present critical Week, which it is hoped will
see a general settlement arrived at. In the cour4
of the afternoon a body of Germans, who have
turned out, marched in procession to the Close,
from Whitechapel, headed by a band of music.
A meeting of the Master Bakers' Trade Pro-
tection Society was held in Anderton's Hotel,
Fleet-street, on Monday night, when Mr. E. S.
Muntz, who presided, expressed an opinion that
the nien,had been too precipitate in the course
they had adopted, and that they could have ob-
tained redress for their grievances in a more
legitimate manner than by a strike. Ultimately
a report was adopted approving generally the pro-
ceedings of the masters' committee, but no ex-
pression of opinion was given as to the future
action of the employers.
There was on Tuesday some subsidence of the
excitement among the operative bakers; and, on
the whole, a more sanguine feeling as to the
ultimate success of their agitation existed. It
appears that the concession of the new principle
by a few considerable firms would give the re-
quired completeness 'to the movement, and with
this object friendly overtures are still being made.
The following is a list of the firms who have men
out upon strike: The mon belonging to the No.
,Branch of the Amalgamated Union; Messrs.
Dove, Brixton ; Johnson, St. Martin's-lane;
Spiking and Co., W.; Mascau, Ilanitnersmith ;
Landrum, Pimlico; Flack, Sloane-street; Selarb,
Chelsea; Finn, Pimlico; Abbott, Waterloo-road;
Croft, Piccadilly ; Shaw, Pimlico ; Atchinson,
Pimlico; Tait, Mount-street ; 13axters,
The strike committee were engaged during the
after part of the day in drawing up a second
manifesto to the public, asking for support, and
the following document was adopted:
_

_
An Appeal for Support to the Nobility, Gentry,
Clergy, Trade Unionists, and Public Generally.
We, the operative bakers of London, have been
agitating for a number of years for the abolition
ot night work and for the recognition of a work-
ing day of twelve hours, not to commence before
four a.m. We have met our employers in con-
ference, as we expected to settle the dispute, but
at the end of the conference, after all the proposi-
tions had been carried in our favour, our em-
ployers told us that they had conceded nothing.
We were therefore compelled to strike to endea-
vour to obtain our just demands, namely, the
adoption of the four to four system, which will
meet all the requirements of the public. In doing
so we heartily believe that we have the sympathy
of the entire community with Us. Some of our
employers have complied with our wishes, we were
compelled in justice to them to withdraw the men
from those shops who will not comply with our
demands, and, in consequence, we have numbers
of men out of employment. We now earnestly
appeal for assistance to help us to support those
men who have sacrificed their situations for a true
and just cause.

A large accession was made on Wednesday to
the list of the unemployed bakers, but no return
of the exact number of the men on strike has yet
been made public. Another effort was made to-
wards the settlement of the dispute by the London
Council, who invited some principals of the
largest firms in the trade to meet and- discuss the
difference at the Admiral Carter, Bartholomew-
close. The invitation was accepted by Messrs.
Hill and Son, Mr. Bonthron, and:Mr. Reid for
Mr. Thornhill, Bishopsgate-street. Mr. Spiking
wrote to decline the interview. Mr. Hill ex-
pressed his willingness to meet the men as far as
possible, but was convinced thathis business could
not be carried on under the four to four system.
Ur, Bonthron cemplained that letter had been

sent to his foreman telling him that he could not
continue to work in the shop, notwithstanding his
expressed intention of giving the new arrangement
a trial, and he had been further annoyed by dis-
covering a piquet placed near his premises. It was
also stated on the part of the employers that
several firms who had tried the four to four plan
had reverted to the old system. On the other
hand, the men contended that their proposals were
in every case feasible, and they pleaded for the
necessity of making no exceptions to the general
rule.

articles.title: AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.
articles.text:
THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.

On Wednesday evening a large meeting of
labourers was -held at the Corn Exchange, Spald-
ing, under the auspices of the South Lincolnshire
Agricultural Union. Great excitement was mani-
fested in the town, and the meeting was inter-
rupted by Mr. Cammoolr, a lawyer, and others.
After several ineffectual appeals from the chair-
man for order, the gentlemen were ejected from
the meeting, amidst the applause of the labourers.
Mr. G. Bailey, of Spalding, presided, and
opened the proceedings in a short speech.

Mr. G. Mitchell, marble rnerchant, of London—
"one from the plough "—in a practical speech
detailed his 'connection with the agricultural
labourers, and showed how they could be elevated
from their present low condition. He 'concluded
by moving the following resolution :
That this meeting deeply sympathises with the
long depressed condition of the agricultural
labourers of this country, and pledges itself to use
every constitutional means in its power to obtain
for them a fair remuneration for their labour ; and
this meeting believes that the only means to ob-
tain this is by forming associations amongst them-
selves for that purpose. Also, that in order to
carry out this resolution, and aid the movement,
immediate steps be taken to procure funds to assist
in the migration and emigration of the labouring
classes.

Mr. Elkins, a labourer, seconded the resolution,
which was supported by Mr. George Potter, and
carried unanimously.
Mr. Ben Taylor, of Peterborough, moved, and
Mr. Balls, of Spalding, seconded the following,
which was also carried :

This meeting views with alarm the recent act
of the Government in sending soldiers into the
harvest field to supplant the agricultural labourer;
there being no scarcity of hands, or refusal by any
to do the work, it also being well known that
in some counties the labourers' pay for harvest
work did not exceed 2s. 6d. per day; and that
Mr. Gladstone be asked to institute an inquiry
into the matter, for the purpose of ascertaining
who is the person responsible for this act, and to
prevent the recurrence of such a stop in the
future.

The meeting closed with hearty votes of thanks
to the speakers and chairman.

A second meeting of the Executive Committee
was held at Leamington on Tuesday, when a
report in reference to emigration was presented.
The Committee decided to render assistance to
suitable persons willing to emigrate, and to pay
their expenses to the port of embarkation. It
was stated that reports had been received that men
were being discharged now that the harvest is in.
From Dorset there was an appeal for leave to
strike, masters having dropped wages in some
cases ss. per week, leaving the men at about Os.,
and desiring the men to hire themselves for
twelve months, a course which the Executive
Committee strongly condemn. The Secretary was
instructed at once to go to Dorset and advise the
men under the circumstances. It was reported
that Mr. Mills, farmer, of Pillerton, had turned
his men out of houses and, allotments; also that
the Rev. Mr. Rose, farmer And magistrate, of
Oxhill, had discharged his men. The united
efforts of these Man have caused some to with-
draw from the union, but the Committee took
courage at seeing that the general tenor of the
people was for the union. It was resolved, in
order effectually to carry out the migration and
emigration schemes of the committee, that
general appeal be made to the pnblic for that
purpose, many having expressed their willingness
to assist in such an enterprise.

The agricultural labourers of Ifundon, follow-
ing in the wake of their neighbours, some time
since joined the Haverhill District Union to a
man. On the 16th instant two of the large gen-
tleman farmers of the place wore somewhat amazed
to find that their men had resolved to strike, and
resist the paltry sum of 1041. for a week's labour.
A remark or two respecting the past of this scat-
tered and uncultivated parish would not perhaps
he out of place. Ilundon, according to the census of
1871, contains 1,116 souls, and has an area of 4,234

acres. The noblemen who occupy the land nor
ride to either church or chapel in their carriages
drawn either by a pair of bays or greys, and enjoyed
some time since conjointly with a parish named
Ridgwell, in the neighbouring county of Essex,
the unenyiahlo notoriety of paying the lowest

wage in the whole district of the eastern counties.
6a. was the priCe, and the poor wretches were
told to keep at home during the bad weather.
The wages the men now demand is only us, per
week, which is sanctioned by the Union. It was
only just before harvest that the men awoke to
the necessity of joining the Union, and acceding
to their request, a deputation from the district,
"Roylti Exchange Haverhill," went over and ad-
dressed the labourers. This caused a great con-
sternation. A visit to this large and overgrown
'village at that time would have well repaid a visit
of a special correspondent from one of the daily
papers, whose graphic description of this abode of
poverty, ignorance, and vice would have awakened
surprise in the eyes a Englishmen. The men
struck for an advanced wage on the 16th, and at
once communicated with the secretary of the dis-
trict. At the end of the week the secretary,
treasurer, and two or three of the committee re-
paired to Hundon, and paid the men on strike 11s.
each, intimating that the funds in hand would be
ample to meet the requirements for several weeks
should the farmers not relent. Such, however,
was not to be the case. One by one the farmers
sent for their serfs, and offered them the full
wages if they returned to their employment. The
result of the matter will bo tested during the
forthcoming winter, as the men are determined
not to yield further, and in default of their
masters not finding them employment, are deter-
mined to follow in the steps of some hundreds of
others who have loft the district, and go to that
hive of well-paid industry, "the North," or emi-
grate to America, the passage to which would be
assisted by the Union. We are pleased to state
that the funds of the Haverhill District Union
"Royal Exchange" is in a prosperoos condition.
The society is well managed, and the members
are proud that a merchant, a disinterested person
at Haverhill, has placed his means and interest to,
and so thoroughly taken up the affairs, of this well
meaning and patriotic service. He may be justly
styled the "labourers' friend," and we wish him
God speed.
The Western .Daily Press publishes two letters
which have passed between the Bishop of
Gloucester and Bristol and Mr. Sotheron Esteourt,
on the subject of the union of agricultural
labourers. The right rev, prelate asks what can
be done by those who are anxious to stay injustice,
and to enable the unfairly treated labourer to
receive his due. He suggests two ways; first, by
sober conferences of employers and employed, in
which unfair treatment and unjust wages might
be brought before the bar of public opinion; and
secondly, by such combination of high-minded
country gentlemen in the form of a county agri-
cultural board, or otherwise, as might express
sound public opinion, and might also exert some
moral force on the hard-dealing and the unjust.
He asks Mr. Estcourt whether there is anything
in these suggestions of which any practical use
could be made. In reply, Mr. Estcourt writes
that, after consideration, he cannot see in what
manner a case can be drawn up for which arbi-
tration could be an effective or a proper remedy.
No doubt, he says, an umpire may be useful in
trade and other commercial undertakings; because
the money value of a man's labour can day by
day be estimated according to the price of the
commodity produced by it; but where, he asks, is
the standard by which an umpire can determine
the value of labour of a farm-servant in any parti-
cular month of the year? The crop is harvested
and made ready for sale only once in a twelve-
month; and it is only by taking an average of the
whole cost and profit, and distributing the amount
over fifty-two weeks, that the value of the
labourer's share can be ascertained. He, however,
thinks it very desirable that public attention
should be drawn from time to time to the subject;
and the bishop has, in his opinion, rendered a
great service to the labourers by affording them
an opportunity of detailing their wants and wishes
under his roof, in his presence, and with liberty of
going fully into the matter.
The fortnightly meeting of the executive of the
National Agricultural Labourers' Union was held
on Monday at the Central Office, Forefield-place,
Leamington. Encouraging reports were received
from the delegates organizing branches and dis-
tricts of the Union in various counties. Mr. J.
Arch had been addressing large meetings by
moonlight in Norfolk; at ono of these Mr. Oldman,
his chairman, was attacked by a farmer, who cut
open his lip by a blow with the fist. The Norfolk
"district" numbers between 20,000 and 30,000.
Mr. E Haynes had been forming branches in
Oxfordshire, Mr. Pill in Berks, and Mr. E.
Russell in Hampshire. Meetings have also been
held during the fortnight in Kent, Cambridgeshire,
Buckingham, Dorset, and other counties. The
roll of membership had been increased to about
260,000, It Irte also reported that the threatened

winter lock-oat had commenced, and that whilst
the aged labourers had to go to the workhouse,
the able-bodied men were being sent to Queens-
land and to the north of England. Three hun-
dred emigrated to New Zealand last week by the
Jessie Readman ; and Messrs. Brogden regularly
ship off 900 a month to their railway works in that
colony. The secretary reported the terms he
had made with the Agent of the Queensland
Colonial Government, so as to secure a free
passage, and a grant of forty acres to each
man. Mr. Taylor also reported that he had visited
Liverpool, West Hartlepool, Sheffield, and other
northern towns, and found that several hundred
men could be employed there at wages ranging
from 18s. to 255. He found that the men already
sent to the North were doing well; only one or
two had returned to Warwickshire. It was do.
cided to carry out emigration and migration with
vigour, so far as funds allowed, in cases where
labourers were discharged for the sin of unionism.
Notwithstanding persecution, bribes, and every
artifice, the Union still advances; the night
meetings, though the air is cold, are enthusiastic;
and the determination increases rather than other-
wise to stick to the Union as the salvation of the
serfs. Mr. Arch has replied to a "tissue of mis-
representations and subterfuges" furnished by
M.P.'s at agricultural dinners. In his address ho
says no sound argument has been brought against
the Union, and all the cavil against the agitators
is but an underhanded blow at the movement, for
labourers Would be gammoned into a make-believe
settlement of the question, and would be bested
in non-union bargains if agitators were to retire at
the bidding of bishops, dukes, and squires. The
agitators would withdraw as mu as the National
Union was firmly established, and the labourers
were competent to conduct the society without aid
from without.

THE RAIL WAY SERVANTS.

The twenty-first half-yearly meeting of the
United_ Kingdom Railway Officers and Servants'
Association and "Railway Provident Society was

articles.title: WORK AND WAGES OF THE LONDON POSTMEN. PART 111.
articles.text:
WORK AND WAGES OF THE
LONDON POSTMEN.
PART 111.

The scale of wages at present in force for letter
carrying is far letter carriers on the town-estab-
lishment 21s. per week, rising by an annual
increment of is., to 255.; remaining at 255. until
twelve years in the service, then rising again by
an annual increment of is. up to 305., taking in
all seventeen years to reach the maximum of 308.
per week.
There are also a large number of young men
and boys whose wages vary from 12s. to 16s. per
week, and in addition some men called auxiliary
letter carriers at fixed wages of 108. The above
scale of wages applies to London letter carriers
only, and is the highest, rate paid. Those on
the suburban, and provincial, and country staff,
although doing an equal, and in many cases a
greater, amount of work, including that curse of
the service, Sabbath labour, receive a smaller
amount of pay, the rule of arrangement appear-
ing to be that those who do the greatest amount of
work shall have the smallest amount of pay, there
actually being men in the country districts in
receipt of no more than Os, weekly, and this for
seven days' labour.

With such low wages, and money, stamps, and
articles of value constantly passing through their
hands, the letter carriers are at times sorely tempted;
and amongst so large a body of men, if we find
some yielding to the temptation, we can scarcly
be surprised. The number of convictions, in pro.
portion to the number of men, employed, is un-
deniably too large; but doubtless by better pay-
ment could ho considerably reduced.
When sorting or stamping in the office, the
men aro constantly watched both by the officers
in the room, and by others, who, though seeing,
are unseen—spy places being contrived in all
directions. One of these, which existed some
years since, in tin Inland Office, consisted of a
bow-window, projecting into the room, glazed
with ground glass; so that a person behind could
look down into the office and see clearly all that
was going on, without being himself seen, should
any one happen to look up. A gentleman con-
nected with the press visited the office, and
subsequently, in his account of it, incidentally
mentioned this window, deprecating the system of
espionage among a body of men generally trust-
worthy.

Soon after, the builders were at work, the bow-
window was taken down, and a largo clock put in
its place. Some of the figures in the dial of this
clock, instead of being painted, were cut com-
pletely through, thus forming quite as good a
peep-hole as did the window, and one which did
not for one day deceive the men as to its real ob-
ject.

The letter carriers are also watched, while on
delivery by officers called street inspectors, and,
when suspicion attaches to them, by the detective
officers also, Case's of dishonesty are only too fre-
quent, in spite of all these precautions, and in spite
of the everity of the sentences upon those con-
victed ; five to seven years' penal servitude being
the minimum of punishment. One man, who had
been more than twenty years in the service, was
sentenced to ten years for stealing a letter con-
taining a penny; and another to four years for
stealing one containing six stamps.
_

Some culprits, however, richly deserve all that
they get. A sorter was once detected taking- a
letter, and upon being searched, a number of
empty envelopes, stamped and addressed, Were
found upon him. Inquiry was nnule at this ad-
dress, and it was then discovered that ho had been
carrying on an artful system of rubbery for more
than three years. He had during that ti rue been
in the regular occupation of two lodgings ; one his
genuine place of residence, the other he had taken
in a false name, stating that he was a commercial
traveller, and should only require the Use of his
room on Sundays, and his letters taken in during
the week. He then provided himself with such
envelopes as were found upon him, and upon corn-
ing across any letters which he conjectured to
contain anything of value, he had only to slip
them into his covers, and so let them pass On to
his second lodging, there to await his arrival at
the end of the week, when he could, of 'course,
open there at his leisure, and in perfect security.
The landlady gave evidence of having taken in
from thirty to forty letters for him every week
during the whole of hi.; stay. If I remember
rightly, his sentence was ten years.
Another
.delinquent, a letter earl ier, whose
operations iippeitt to have been as extensive, but
net So cleverly- conducted, was discovered in a
somewhat curious manner. The officers of the
detective department appear to have had no sus-
picion of him whatever; but it happened that in
changing his lodgings he, with that suicidal care-
leesne4,l which seems to bs eliaratiteristic of some

criminals, neglected to take with him two hat-
boxes, which he had crammed full of stolen
letters. After he had gone, the landlady, in
cleaning the room, found these boxes, and, com-
municating with the Post-Office, his axprehension
and conviction of course followed.

articles.title: BLAST FURNACEMEN.
articles.text:
THE BLAST FURNACEMEN.

A meeting of blast furnacemen was held on
Tuesday night at the Swan Hotel, Iligh-street,
Dudley. There were men present from all parts
of South Staffordshire, and the meeting was held
for the purpose of agitating for the adoption by
the masters of the eight hours' system, and also to
advocate organization. Several speakers com-
plained that nearly every other branch had had
their hours of labour reduced, and now it was the
blast furnacemen's turn to be considcred.—Mr.
Walker (member of the Ironworkers' Council of
Arbitration) strongly advocated organization, and
affirmed that the time had arrived for every trade
in the country to be attached to one grand
national association. But, of course, they must go
on by degrees, and he was there that evening to
invite the blast furnacemen to join the Iron-
workers' Association, so that when the present
system was revised, the grievances of all branches
of the trade might be discussed and settled.—A
resolution was proposed and carried, that a branch
lodge of the association be formed in Dudley.

articles.title: COAL MINERS.
articles.text:
THE COAL MINERS.

FIFESIIIRE.

Great meetings of miners were held throughout
Fifeshira on Saturday, at which it was reported
that at three different collieries the masters had
conceded the full demands of the men, who were
accordingly working on the advance of is. 9d, per
day. With regard to the other collieries, however,

It was determined to adhere to the former resolu-

articles.title: CLAYCROSS.
articles.text:
CLAYCROSS.

The miners in the employ of the Claycross Com-
pany are agitating for an advance of wages and
the redress of several grievances. A deputation
from thorn have had an interview with Mr. Ilium,
general manager, and their grievances were pro-
mised consideration. As to wages, ho said a
reduction was as probable as an advance. lie
would not care if all the principal collieries stood a
week, as both markets and cellars were full. The
united sale at five of the company's markets
last week only amounted to 200 tons. The state
of the markets had compelled the company to put
their own main pits on short time. Referring to
the union which the men are busy forming amongst
themselves, Mr. liinns said if they were determined
to go on with it lie should raise their rents, shut up
their schools, and cease certain of their allowances.
In short, he should oppose the movement, and he
refused to hear a member of the deputation on
account of his connection with the union.

articles.title: BRASSFOUNDRY TRADE.
articles.text:
THE BRASSFOUNDRY TRADE.

A meeting in connection with the Chandelier
and Gasfitting Masters' Association was held on
Tuesday at the Great Western Hotel, Birmingham,
for the purpose of considering the demand of the
men for an advance of 15 per cent. on their wages.
Mr. H. Heaton presided.
After some deliberation, the following resolution,
which the committee had prepared, was unani-
mously adopted :

" That, although strongly maintaining the prin-
ciple of a revision of the prices rather than a
bonus, yet, desirous of avoiding the serious con-
sequences which must arise from a strike alike to
the employers and employed, this association accede
to the advance of 16 per cent."
On Tuesday night a meeting of the delegates
in the brass trade was held at the Zion School-
room, Newhall-street, Birmingham.- A communi-
cation was received from the employers, inviting
a deputation of the men's committee to meet them
at their rooms, at seven o'clock, and intimated
that they had conceded the 15 per cent. as a bonus,
and wished to confer with them as to the time
when it should conic into operation. The com-
mittee of the society accordingly met them at the
appointed time,

Mr. Thews read a resolution of the employer, to
the effect that the 15 per cent. advance should
come into operation on December 1.

After some friendly discussion, it was decided
that the advance should come into operation on
November 1.

The conference concluded with a vote of thanks
to the employers' deputation, who expressed a wish
that tho friendly feeling then prevailing might be
of long aumtion,

articles.title: TIN PLATE WORKERS.
articles.text:
THE TIN PLATE WORKERS.

The position of the tin-plate trade in South
Wales has become very unsatisfactory. Owing to
the decreased demand for tin plates and the high
prices of all the raw materials used in the manu-
facture, the makers have unanimously determined
to reduce the make one-third, by working only
four days per week instead of six, rather than sell
their manufacture at lower prices than they have
lately obtained. This determination has given rise
to disaffection among the tin plate workers, and
a general strike is impending. With the prospect
of having the wages of two days' labour weekly
cut off from them they claim a higher rate of re-
muneration for the four days' labour; and what
they principally demand is, that the ton shall be
the legitimate 20cwt., and not 21ewt., which the
employers have been accustomed to claim. The
tin plate masters in the Swansea and Briton Ferry
districts firmly decline to concede the demand, and
the result is that several of the works are at a
standstill.

articles.title: PRIVATE DWELLING HOUSES AT THE VIENNA EXHIBITION.
articles.text:
PRIVATE DWELLING HOUSES AT
THE VIENNA EXHIBITION.

At the Universal Exhibition_, to be held at
Vienna in 1873, the private dwelling house
will have the importance of forming a group
to itself. This group has been destined to
help to solve one of the most important ques-
tions of social science of the day. Its object is
not to exhibit a collection of ethnographical
objects, neither is it to show how most of the
private dwelling houses are built and arranged
in different countries, but to show how the
private dwelling house can and ought to be
built in order best to fulfil its purpose, taking
into consideration the climate, local circum-
stances, and mode of life of the different
peoples, as well as their wants and habits.
One very common error, for instance,
hitherto in undertakings with the special ob-
ject of providing houses for working men, has
been the construction of huge nests of bricks
and mortar, in which there is no private
ownership beyond the two or three rooms
enclosed within a separate door, ard a right
of way down a common staircase. Whatever
may be the architectural or economical advan-
tages of this kind of building, it has one fatal
fault. It is not liked, and there is no reason
to suppose that it ever will be liked, by the
persons who are intended to benefit by it. It
is very doubtful whether the flat system has
any future in London even for the richer
classes. The experiment begun in Victoria-
street has not been often repeated, and where
it has been, the system has usually developed
into a mere-modification of hotel life: Besides,
the unfortunately unavoidable consequences of
the living of many in a small space, and of the
thus loosened family life, manifest themselves
in the injury of health and morality.
It is for that reason that we see everywhere
endeavours made to restore again the old
family house, but arranged to suit the require-
ments of tnedern life.

The group destined to represent the private
dwelling,house (Ist) by models, drawings, and
finished buildings, and. (2nd) by drawings,
models, and examples of thoroughly furnished
apartments at the Vienna Exhibition, will
show the rooms, the kitelien, the cellar, &c.,
with all the requirements of housekeeping, and
all most approved arrangements as a whole and
ready for immediate use, and thus present to
the visitor an arrangement which cannot by
any other means be exhibited in so complete
or clear a manner, and which imagination can
never represent to itself.
This Exhibition will enable the architects of
all civilized nations to exhibit the private
dwelling houses which suit best the climate
and habits of their country, and also enable
visitors, who give their attention to this
problem, to make instructive comparisons, and
to adept the arrangements which may be
suited to their own country and customs.
It is intended that the houses exhibited,
besides being fully and completely furnished
' and decorated, shall be likewise as far as
practicable inhabited.
The art of the joiuer and cabinet-
maker, the upholsterer, the painter, the potter,
&q,. will appear side by aide, and appeal
collectively by the technical skill and. taste
displayed. to the approval of the visitor.

One particular feature of prominent interest
to English manufacturers and exhibitors
deserves to be specially noticed in connection
with this group.
Iron constructions are almost unknown in
Austria', and it, may be taken for certain that
if introduced by. enterprising firms (and such
are,not wanting in England), they would meet
with a ready sale. .Even a very profitable
investment might be made by erecting several
of these iron houses previously to the opening
of the Exhibition, for it is a well-known fact
to residents in Vienna that at present there is
not• enough accommodation for the resident
Population, and that in consequence rents are
enormously high.
By the exhibition of these iron construc-
tions the manufacturer will derive a double
advantage. In the first place he will be re-
ceiving rent for the houses whilst they are in-
habited; and, secondly, it will perhaps do more
to convinoe Vienna capitalists and building
societies of the practicability of iron houses
than all advertisements in the world. Let
their superiority teatime or brick constructions
once be allowed, and numerous orders will be
sure to follow.

The houses, however, which are mostly re-
quired at Vienna are not those enormous ten
and twelve storey structures which are familiar
to every one who has visited Continental
cities. The most urgent want of the people
there is a good transportable dwelling for
working men, containing from two to four
rooms, and others with one room and a kitchen
only, suitable for man and wife.
Such buildings are almost unknown in
Vienna, and considering that the town has a
very large labouring population, they are as
much needed as elsewhere. To men employed
in large manufaotories a dwelling of this kind
would b peeially acceptable, for, on account
of want of good accommodation and the very
high rents which prevail ía a densely popu-
lated district, the Austrian artizaus and
Uleohallios have often a diAance of throe or

four English miles to walk morning and even-

ing.
Summers and winters in Austria are more
severe than in England, and hence the greater
need of a decent dwelling nearer the man's
daily work. Many of the manufactories there
have plenty of spare ground, which they now
appropriate to depositing rubbish, but which,
in many instances, would be available for the
erection of constructions as heretofore sug-
gested.
Ordinary building materials are very dear
at Vienna; bricks cost from 30 to 35 florins
(50 to 60 shillings) per 1,000, and other
materials are in the same proportion. Ac-
cording to the opinion of others who are well
informed in such matters, iron dwelling houses
imported from England, after cost of carriage,
customs' duty, and all charges are paid, in-
cluding erection, will not be dearer than brick
constructions of the same character. One very
important advantage in their favour is the
rapidity with which they can be erected, and
in the interest of the working-man and poorer
classes, the co-operation of manufacturers in
England, France, and elsewhere is earnestly
solicited by the Austrian people.

articles.title: LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.
articles.text:
THE LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.

The usual meeting was held on Wednesday
at the Guildhall, Lord Lawrence presiding.
A report was brought up in reference to the
Bath-street and Radnor-street schools, some
discussion ensuing thereon. Eventually, the
report was adopted; but Mr. Luoraft gave
notice that he should open up the subject
again at the next meeting by, movinq that it
Is necessary to have a Board school in every
one of the four divisions in which Radnor-
street is situated. The Chairman suggested
that words should be added to the motion to

. _
the effect that the question as to whether the
Radnor-street schools should be retained or
not be left over for the present. This met
with general approval, and the motion, with
this addendum, was agreed to.
Mr. Charles Reed, M.P., moved:

That it be an instruction to the managers of
Board schools to report to the Board as to the
number of places which could be assigned without
charge to destitute children whose parents are un-
able to pay the school fee. 2. That a letter be
addressed by the Board to the managers of public
elementary schools in London, suggesting that
where there are vacancies in such schools, a
certain proportion of places should be set apart,
without charge, for one year, and under the con-
ditions laid down by the resolution of the Board
of the 2nd clay of November, 1871, for children
whose parents the manager have ascertained by
their own inquiries, or on the certificate of the
Board, to be unable to pay the school fee, and
that the provision thus made be reported to the
Board. That the proposed Bye-Law VIII. be
withdrawn, and that the Board resolves that, for
twelve months from the present date, remission or
payment of fees in public elementary schools shall
be made exceptionally on proof of urgent tem-
porary need, each case being dealt with on its own
merits, without prejudice to the principles involved
on either side, it being understood that such re-
mission or payment of fees is not to be considered
as made in respect of any instruction in religious
subjects.
In consequence of the small number of
members present, it was agreed to allow the
matter to be postponed for a fortnight.

articles.title: PERSONAL RIGHTS.
articles.text:
PERSONAL RIGHTS.

We are requested to publish the following
memorial of the Executive Committee of the
Vigilance Association for the Defenoe of Per-
sonal Rights, to the Right Hon. W. E. Glad-
stone, M.P., First Lora of Her Majesty's
Treasury :=

Saii,—We desire respectfully to address you,
and to express and explain the grounds of our
apprehension in regard to a species of legislation
which has occupied a very large part of the late
and previous parliamentary sessions, and which
promises to attain still greater prominence, and
and to create a new and radical division in public
opinion. Before instancing particular measures,
we may characterise this legislation as entailing a
considerable extension of the powers and duties of
the Executive, as it enters into the municipal, or
parochial, and in some instances the domestic life
of the community, beyond the present limits of
imperial legislation.
We premise that, in our opinion,' this nation is
mainly indebted for the extraordinary stability of
its political system, and its comparative immunity
from social disturbance, to the existing system of
localised administration. We find in our muni-
cipal and parochial systems the main source of the
self-reliance, prudence, and publics spirit, which
renders the people of the United Kingdom pre-
eminent in their capacity for self-government.
And we believe that if popular legislation is to
escape failure, or even to continue to exist in
reality, the people must not be deprived, in any
considerable degree, of the discipline afforded by
the administration of their own laws. We refer,
in corroboration of this opinion, to the views of
many leading reformers in France, Spain, and
other European countries, who base their en-
deavours to obtain popular in place of despotic
government on the discontinuance of that central-
isation which is the necessary obverse of the
latter. We refer, in particular, to the proposal
for the resumption of their municipal powers by
the department, arrondissement, canton, and com-
mune, which has recently issued, as binding its
eandidetes, from the Democratic Committee vital).

lished in Paris—and to the measures proposed by
the Committee of Decentralisation, nominated by
the present Government of France.
We also approve the close identification of the
Executive with the Legislature which has hitherto
been maintained in our political system; and we
consider that it is essential to the continuance of
this system, and to the effective maintenance of
the responsibility of the Ministry of Parliament,
that the work of the former should not be so
largely extended as to render the present method
of government impracticable. We apprehend,
also, that the multiplicity of the demands which
are now made upon the attention of the Ministry,
and of Parliament, seriously impedes and delays
reforms which are urgently required in otir legal
code and judicial system, as well as the efficient
defence of the country.
We consider, further, that the system of muni-
cipal taxation and expenditure provides an in-
valuable guarantee, for economy*, and the best
security against an extravagance which would be
liable to lead to illusive and demoralizing expedi-
ents, especially in connection with the legal pro-
vision for the poor. We should therefore regard
with grave fear any large substitution of imperial
for local taxation, or infringement of our system
of municipal control over the latter.
We regard as an evil the multiplication of
Government places and minor officials, not only on
account of the notorious danger of official corrup-
tion, but as tending to withdraw public servants
from the legitimate effect of public opinion, to
lessen the sense of individual responsibility, and
to weaken public!, opinion itself, and thereby to
retard that social progress which depends on a
general elevation of the popular intelligence.
In regard to the sanitary legislation proposed
by the Public Health Act and other projected
measures, while we are deeply conscious of the
importance of the ends proposed, and while we
recognise the utility of one or more centres for the
purpose of general guidance and the circulation of
information we regard the system, under which
the municipal and parochial bodies are completely
responsible, as possessing an exceptional advantage
in rendering the care of their health the object of
individual endeavour and intelligent interest on
the part of the people, in the greatest degree com-
patible with any external control. At the same
time, in view of the provision contained in the act
referred to, rendering obligatory the appointment
of medical officers of health and,other sanitary
officers, and of the various proposals to vest in
such officers larger and more arbitrary powers than
have hitherto been deemed expedient, we state our
belief that great evil must attend such control, if
it is made or should become unduly extensive and
strict. We fear that tlao coercion proposed Will,
by its excess, defeat the object of these measures;
both by impairing the will and the ability of the
people to interest themselves individually in the
care of their own health, and by bringing odium
upon the system so prescribed and enforced.
We would urge that to accustom the people to
protect their own health is of greater ultimate
importance than any advantage which may be
more immediately attainable; and, while we
appreciate the zeal and the service of the-medical
faculty, we are of opinion that this, the paramount
object, has been overlooked, and is narrow and
false view has been taken, in the pretensions which
a lo.re portion of the faculty have advanced in '
relation to this and other measures, with what
appears to us an indecent eagerness for the ad-
vancement of their professional interests, and a
wholly unlawful ambition to place themselves in
the position of masters and legislative dictators to -
the community, whilst we especially resent the
presumptuous efforts of a portion of the medical
profession to force upon the people, against their
ascertained will, the maintenance and extension of
the Contagious Diseases Acts.
In view of the countenance which these pre-
tensions have received from a portion of the
present House of Commons, and of the pro-
nounced antagonism, in regard to these last-named
measures, which is known to exist between the
majority of that House and the majority of the
electorate and the people, we desire to express,
our strong conviction of the vital necessity
of maintaining the principle of the responsi-
bility of the Legislature to the electoral
body, as opposed to the so-called education of the
people through the alien instrumentality of the
Legislature, as alone justifying our system of re-
preson•tative government, and enabling it to fulfil
its direct object of providing for the redress of
social grievances, and its indirect object, the moral
and intellectual discipline of as large a propor-
tion of the people as it may be expedient to en-
franchise. We" would urge the presumption
which exists against all legislation which implies
a denial of this responsibility--aul which sub-
ordinates and delays great measures of social
justice, and checks or deadens the movements of
public opinion, in which they originate.
We 'earnestly deprecate, as a disgraceful retrogres-
sion and a fatal evil, the multiplication of restric-
I tions On personal liberty—which appears to be
threatened in greater or loss degree by the super-
vision provided for on the part of the police, or of
medical or other agents of the Executive, in several
of the measures meutioned below. We would
protest against such restrictions, especially on
account of their injustice to the poor, whose
homes are thereby rendered , exceptionally liable
to vexatious and tyrannical molestation.

In view of the several dangers, which to us ap-
pear imminent, we would urge the following pre-
cautions as of vital importance in the perilous arta
almost unprecedented course of legislation which
has been commenced.

_
1. That the constitutional guarantees of per-
aqua liberty should in no case be violated.
2. That the imposition, direct or indirect, of
exneptional burdens or restrictions on any particu-
lar section of the community, should be jealously
avoided.

3. That the multiplication of criminal offences
should he regarded as in itself a certain cause of
future CXUfIC awl permanent demoralisation and
that the treatment of any ttots as grimitial, Which

are not in themselves necessarily such, should be
avoided with the utmost possible consistency.
4. That any law sluiuld be considered
ineffectual and suicidal which tends to annihilate
the criminal the hope of social reinstatement.
G. That the laws proposed should, whenever it
may be 'possible contain or point to the means of
prevention of the social evils against which such
laWs are directed; and in no case, for any
purpose whatever,. tend to counteract those means
of prevention in which the general judgment of
society confides. ,
6. That, in the fulfilment of the trust vested in
Parliament and its duty to tho unrepresented, in
all domestic or social legislation, in which the
interests of women are directly or indirectly con-
cerned, the ascertained sentiments of women
should guide and restrain the Legislature, and
that, where meral considerations enter into the
subject of legislation, whether immediately or
remotely, the standard generally adopted by women,
as well as that of men, should be carefully and
respectfully regarded.
We are of opinion that one or more of those
precautions has been neglected in each of the
following measures lately under consideration of
or ratified by Parliament :—The Prevention of
Crime Act, the Pedlars' Act, the Act fpr the Pro-
tection of Infant Life, the Criminal Law Amend-
ment Act, the Habitual Drunkards Bill, the Public
Prosecutors Bill; the Contagions Diseases Pre-
vention Bill, and, in our opinion, these precautions
are each and all signally and scandalously discarded
in the existing Contagious Diseases Acts. We
condemn such legislation not only _as contrary to

A CHINESE DISH.

When our party of six had seated themselves at
the centre table, my attention was attracted by a
covered dish—something unusual at a Chinese
meal. On a certain signal the cover was re-
moved, and presently the face of the table was
covered with juvenile crabs, which made their ex-
odus from the dish with all possible rapidity. The
crablets had been thrown into a plate of vinegar
just as the company sat down—such an immersion
making them more brisk and lively than usual.
But the sprightly sport of the infant crabs was soon
checked by each guest seizing what he could, dash-
ing it into his mouth, crushing it between his teeth,
and swallowing the whole morsel without core •
mony. Determined to do as the Chinese did, I tried
this novelty also with one or two. I succeeded,
finding the shell soft and gelatinous, for they were
tiny creatures, not more than a day or two old.
But I was compelled to give in to the third, which
had resolved to take vengeance, and gave my
lower lip a nip so sharp and severe as to make me
relinquish my hold, and likewise to dcsist from any
further experiment of this nature.

In the eulogy delivered by the Rev. Dr.

good of' man." He concludes as follows :

"'lt does not matter how a man dies; the
matter is, how he lived.' God knows that cir-
cumstances in providence may happen to deprive
,Ine of my reason. No man has any more security
fcr his reason than he has for his life; and cir-
cumstances may deprive me of my reason, and I
may, in the whirlwind of uncontrolled and un-
governable passion, and when the helmsman has
been swept away from his post, do what I would
never have done in my calm and collected

never happen—and God be thanked for it, for it

the connection between the two members of this
sentence shall never be severed—' For me to live

how, come death when, come death where it may,
this hope still remains—to me to live is Christ,

A French officer, who had served in Algiers,
and had formerly been employed by the Govern-
ment in Constantinople, relates the following in-
stance of the manner in which justice is frequently
administered in Turkey by the inferior judges
when debts are claimed by foreigners:

"A manufacturer of Carcassone arrived at Con-
stantinople with a large investment of cloths, which,
by a new process, he had rendered peculiarly fit
for the Turkish market. An Armenian dealer
was so pleased with the goods that he bought the
whole lot, and paid by his note of hand at short
date. When the note matured the merchant
called upon the Turk to receive payment for the
amount of the note, but his surprise may be well
imagined when the Turk told him that ho had
already paid it, and owed him nothing.
"'But,' remonstrated the merchant, 'here is
your note, which I should have given to you if
you had paid it.'
"' It is of no consequence,' responded the
Armenian. I have paid it, and can produce my
witnesses to prove the payment.'
"In this dilemma the merchant felt that no
resource was left but to seek the aid of the French
Ambassador, who, feeling the inefficiency of his
own intervention, recommended him to place his
case in the hands of one of his own interpreters,
who understood pretty well the chicanery of the
Turkish law, and was aware of the system pursued
by native debtors to elude the payments of demands
for which they were liable.
"When measures were prepared the merchant
and his debtor appeared before the Judge, whe de-
manded of the former his ground ef complaint.
" ' The payment of this note," he replied, which
he claims of have discharged.'
"'What do you reply to this?' asked the Judge
of the debtor.

" ' That I have already paid it, and that here are
my witnesses.'
"Truly enough, two men advanced from the
crowd, and testified circumstantially to the payment
of the note, mentioning the dayiand hour when it
took place.
"The affair seemed decided, and the consterna-
tion of the plaintiff was completo, when the inter-
preter, who had remained silent, thus addressed
the Judge:
" We admit the payment of the note, as stated
by these worthy men; but they have failed to toll
you, or perhaps did not know, that in one hour
after, we lent the money back to the defendant for
his accommodation.'
"To corroborate this statement two wittfesses
stepped forth, and bore as full testimony as the
two former had done on the opposite side. And,
as the defendant was unable to rebut them, he
was obliged to satisfy the demand. This is fully
up to the modern practice in some more civilized
lands."

Rare almost as great poets—rarer, perhaps,
than veritable saints nnd martyrs—are consum-
mate men of business. A mail, to be excellent in
this way, must not only be variously gifted, but
his gifts should be nicely proportioned to one
another. He must have, in a high degree, that
Nirtue which men have always found the least
pleasant of virtues—prudence. His prudence,
however, will not be merely of a cautious and
quiescent order, but that which, being ever
actively engaged, is more fitly called discretion
than prudence. Such a man must have an almost
ignominious love of details, blended (and this is a
rare combination) with a high power of imagina-
tion, enabling him to look along extended lines of
possible action, and put these details in their right
places. 1-To requires a great knowledge of cha-
racter, with that exquisite tact which feels
unerringly the right moment when to act. A
discreet rapidity must pervade all the movements
of his thought and action. He must be singularly
free from vanity, and is generally found to be an
enthusiast who has the art to conceal his enthu-
siasm.

FOOD AND DIGESTION.

There can be no doubt that the palate is designed
to inform us what is proper for the stomach, and,
of course, that must beat instruct us what food to
take and what to avoid; we want no other adviser.
Nothing can be more clear than that those articles
which are agreeable to the taste were by nature
intended for our food and sustenance, whether
liquid or solid, foreign or of native production. If
they are pure and unadulterated, no harm can be
dreaded by their use: they will only injure by
abuse. Consequently, whatever the palate ap-
proves, eat and drink always in moderation, but
never in excess ; keeping in mind that the first pro-
cess of digestion is performed in the mouth, the
second in the stomach; and that, in order that the
stomach may be able to do its work properly, it is
requisite the first process should he well performed.
This consists in masticating, or chewing the solid
food, so as to break down and separate the fibres
and small substances of meat and vegetables, mix-
ing them well, and blending the whole together
before they are swallowed; and it is particularly
urged upon all to take plenty of time to their
meals, and never eat in haste.

MARVELS OF TUE INSECT WORLD. - Man ;
generally flatters himself that his anatomy is about
the highest effort of Divine skill; yet that of the
insect is far more complicated. No portion of our
organism can compare with the proboscis of the
common fly. Man can boast 370 muscles. Lyonet,
who spent his whole life in watching a single
species of caterpillar, discovered in it 4,000. The
common fly has 8,000 eyes, and certain butterflies
25,000. M. Pouchet treats it as an established
fact that so fine are the sensory organs of ants,
that they converse by means of their antennoo.
Consequently, the strength and activity of insects
far surpass ours in proportion. In the whole
field of natural science there is nothing more
astouniing than the number of times a fly can flap
its wings in a second. As the fly passes through
space at the rate of six feet in a second, it must in
that point of time vibrate its wings five or six
hundred times. But in rapid flight we are re-
quired to believe that 3,600 is a moderate estimate.
The mind is stupifled if it attempts to realise these
results.

INSTANCES OP VELOCITY.—The rapidity of the
transmission of the nervous agent along the nerves
(whether motor or sensory) is by no means so
great as is popularly supposed, and cannot boar
the slightest comparison with other velocities
with which physicians are acquainted. The
velocity of electricity is at least 500,000,000
yards in one second; that of light, according to
late corrections, is 325,000,000 yards; that of
shooting stars upwards of 70,000 yards; that of
sound, ~,transmitted along iron, 5,607, and
transmitted through the air, 364 yards; that of an
eagle at its quickest flight, 88 yards. The
velocity of the nervous agent is from 28 to 33
yards, which is between the velocity of the eagle
and that of the racehorse or greyhound. "Hence,"
as Professor flu Bois-Reymond observes, "in the
racehorse and greyhound, when they are running
at full speed, the nervous agent will nearly rest
in space, because its motion is destroyed by the
rapid onward progression of the animal; and in
the flying eagle it will even be carried in the
opposite direction. As in these cases, the whole
body of the animal is darted through space at a
rate equal, or oven superior, to that of the nervous
agent, it will be less a matter of surprise that man
is able to move his hand almost 48 quickly as that
agent moves along his nerves."
THE ATMOSPIIERE.—When the atmosphere is
in rapid notion, we call it the" wind ;" but when
its motion is gentle, we speak of it as the "air."
The term "gale" is applied to intense velocity of
the atmosphere. Wore it not for the motion of
the atmosphere the ocean would be a vast, calm

lake, with the exception of its tidal currents. A I
storm at sea is a striking illustration of the power
of the wind. We can also see its effocts in driving
corn-mills, and up-rooting trees; but its powers is
btill more manifest when it lifts millions of tons of
water into waves, and the sea becomes furious.
The pressure of the wind upon the waves depends
upon its velocity. During a gale, or hurricane, it
travels at the rate of more than 100 feet in a
second, or about one mile in a minute, and it gives
a pressure equal to about 12 lb. per square foot.
A. wall, a sail, or a wave, by its square surface,
can therefore give an estimate as to the force of
the wind upon it. When the atmosphere moves
at about 7 feet in a second the wind is moderate;
at 30 feet it is fresh ; at 60 feet is strong; at 80
to 90 feet it is a tempest. In England the average
velocity of air is about 20 feet every second. The
land and sea breeze which is experienced in our
island, perhaps more than in any other part of the
world, is caused by the wind blowing from the sea
during the day, and during the night from land.
The movements of the atmosphere are so regular
in some parts of the earth, and periodical in
others at stated seasons, that the winds have
definite names, such as monsoons, sirocco, trade
winds, &c.
