THE STRIKE AT MESSRS. CORBETT'S

AND M'CLYMONT'S.

THE conduct Of Messrs. CORBETT and
M'CLYMONT is one of the strongest justifica-
tions of trades unionism. Were there not the
rivalry of an overcrowded labour market to
cause competition between the man out of
work and those in work, matters might move
On satisfactorily enough in regard to wages,
as each man would then have the power to
make a satisfactory bargain for himself. Or
were employers not disposed, as they are, to
cut under each other in the market, wages need
not be unnaturally depressed to meet the
requirements of those who are determined to
take possession of custom by cheapness.
But seeing that every branch of business is
afflicted by such dishonourable competitors,
who, so as they gain customers, are indifferent
as to whether the workman starves or not, it is
necessary to meet them by the organized power
of union, that honourable employers may not
be compelled to follow their, bad example to
prevent themselves from being driven out of
the market. Messrs. CORBETT and M'CLymosp
seem to be speculative builders, to whom low
wages is a matter of great moment. To get
on they must be lower in their prices than
their honourable rivals. Their profit does not
appear to arise from a surplus over a fair
price paid for good work, but by cutting down
the wages of the unfortunate people in their
employ. Just as in the middle ages dishonest
traders increased their gain by clipping the
coin.

These men, after a long struggle, and when
the general body of the trade had agreed to

certain conditions, refuse to conform to the
settlement made, and have thus forced on the

men in their employment a second strike.
Whatever there is of folly or iniquity in
this cannot be charged against the men; it is a

wanton effort on the part a CUILBETT and
11.'CLYmoNT to break away from the agree-
ment made, that they may pocket all they can
take from their workers, and thus be enabled
to tender under rivals by the advantage low
wages gives them.

The -workmen are bound to resist this in

the interest of their fellow workers, and the
other employers ought to make it a duty on
their part, in their own interest, to help the
men. Outside of this all working men should
make the quarrel their own, and pour abun-
dant contributions into the coffers from which

the men on strike are to be paid. Employers
who act on the principle which seems to regu-

late the conduct of Messrs. CORBETT and
3.l.'Cr.vmosT are the pests of trade, they are a
curse to the men and a plague to their fellow'
employers. They beat down wages by
fighting the men out of work against the men
in work, and they reduce fair profits by their
shabby success in securing cheapness of pro-
duction by clipping wages. Their existence 0
employers is a standing menace to working
men, and all legitimate and legal action that
can be used to force such persons on to the
same ground as their honourable rivals in
trade ought to be resorted to for that
.purpose.
,The first thing, however, is for all working
men, to subscribe liberally in support of the
strike, and the next is to assist everywhere to
increase the number of men in the various
trades societies, as to provide for surplus
labour by union funds is to take the necessi-
tous working man out of such hands as those
of CORBETT and M'CLYMONT, as it is fronl
these they derive their power to carry on the
ignoble game by which they grow rich.

THE GREAT CONSTITUTIONAL PARTY

AT PRESTON.

THE Preston election forces itself back 011
our attention for reasons apart from any effect
it may have on the condition of our two great
rival political parties. It has always been the
boast of honest Englishmen, that whether the
law they live under was the best that could be
divised or not, to obey it, so long as it
remained unchanged, and act uprightly 111
accord,ance with its opirit, was their WeAt.

The Conservatives, it must be confessed, are
the loudest in this kind of profession— :
their reverence has caused them to go in
for even the oldest and the worst. A true
Conservative would stand up for the drat de
clam which empowered the feudal lord to :
thrust his booted leg into the bed of the newly
married couple in assertion of his right. How :
is it, then, that this ballot law has turned them
into scheming tricksters against legality?
In this case we have Mr. GORST, at Preston,
setting in motion a deliberately-planned
scheme to defeat the law—a scheme which
would be highly creditable to a burglar plan-
ning the plunder of a house; but which to
the manager of the great Conservative party
is ah ineffaceable disgrace. There is not
in the rascally tag rag which hangs on to
all parties, but which, for the sake of what
It can get, belongs almost naturally to
the Conservative party—a scoundrel with
active faculties who may not take heart from
the conspicuous example of Mr. GOP,ST the groat
Conservative agent, and apply himself in any
way to cheat the law for his own benefit.
This gentleman went to Preston to drive a
coach and six through the law in the interest
of his party, but his followers, encouraged by
his example, may take upon themselves to
cheat it in their own interest. What has
turned to the honour and advantage of Mr,
Gonsp, may come to others as clipped hair.
prison-suits, and the tread-wheel. Does Mrs
DISRAELI know of this? Is he the great
modern political MERCURY, who embraces
the people to rob them of their political
honesty, as the ancient thief stole the girdle of
VENUS whilst she caressed him ? If the
tricks practiced by Mr. GOUST and his friends
at Preston are to be repeated, they must
be met by similar shifts; as the Liberals can,
in a political sense, be as scoundrelly as their
Conservative rivals, and if they cannot work
the matter as Mr. GonsT and his Conservative
friends did, they must try some other plan.
The history of our open English election,
will suggest many ways of meeting one species
of rascality by another. When the Conserva-
tive agents take up their posts at the polling
booths, an organized gang of ardent half-
drunken Liberals might set on them with
bludgeons, and belabour them soundly; or if
there was a river at hand they might pitch
them into it. Hanging them from lamp-posts
would be too severe a punishment, though it
would be a great gain to the public. If Mr.
GLADSTONE and Mr. DISRAELI, or even Mr.
GLYNN and Mr. GORST, think it right to go
into a little game of this kind, they had better
play it out spiritedly. The great constitutional
" national " party have set the example, and it
cannot, therefore, be wrong to follow it. If
Major GERMAN, who was beaten by the in-
trigues of Mr. GOUST at Preston, should
bonnet Mr. DISRAELI in Palace Yard, it would
only be keeping tho jollity up, and a general
scrimmage would only increase the fun. If
we are to be countenanced in biting the law
by the nose, when we would force it, as
SHAKESPEARE says, so be it; let the general
scrimmage come, there are yet in England
teeth to be knocked out, and heads to be
broken, scamps to be bribed, and rascals to
bribe them; poor wretches to be coerced, and
rich knaves to coerce them. Let the game be
played out, and let us, if we must, go on
shuffling and cutting in the best way we can.
Law is a slow and sometimes a most unsatis-
factory method of putting things right. A bit of
rough and tumble for the ballot may give the
people the additional opportunity of putting
a few other matters right.
Mr. DISRAELI and Mr. GORST are, we think,
playing with edged tools. They have won
the Preston election by laughing at the law,
and may win others in the same way; but
beyond these there are numbers of matters
connected with the political situation of the
country which they ought not to put to risk
by indulging in a too transparent game of
party thimblerig.

articles.title: OLD CATHOLICS.
articles.text:
THE OLD CATHOLICS.

TILE old Catholic party is seeking to find
grounds of agreement between itself and the
anti-papal communities, which, if found, are by
no means certain to lead to any very useful
result. Dr. DOLLINGER and his friends are
Lii antagoniem with Rome, hut that i no

proof that they can put themselves into agree-
ment with bodies of Protestants who occupy
ground which the old Catholics of Germany
do not seem anxious to take up. We cannot
see that the Cologne Conference will lead to
much, because we cannot forget how difficult
it is for religious bodies, however wide or
narrow their differences, to dwell together in
Christian brotherhood.

• The Church of Rome feels how impossible
it is to hold intact its old dogmas with its old
grip in the presence of modern thought.
Councils and mandates are alike powerless for
this purpose, and whether that Church at-
tempts concession, or indulges in asserting
and reasserting old dogmas, the same disinte-
grating influence is at work, crumbling its
authority away, RS the action of the winds and
the waters waste even the granite ribs of
the world.

The very existence of Dr. DOLLINGEII and

his party shows the altered and dangerous
condition of tho Roman Catholic Church. But

this by no means gives evidence of any power
of Christian cohesion in the various reformed
Churches by which it is assailed; nor do we
see in either Dean STANLEY'S letter, or that of
the Bishop of LINCOLN, any proof that a new
Protestant unity can borput in the place of the
old Catholic unity, now no longer to be found.
The world has got utterly sick of the old
corporate authority, so exacting and oppres-
sive at Rome, which so utterly subordinated
freedom of individual thought to collective
decisions, frequently antagonistic to the wel-
fare of the world, and so often opposed to
plain truth and common sense.

In regard to the unity of spiritual truth, we
have no desire to argue such a question. It
may be possible to get at absolute agree-
ment as to doctrine in the Christian world,
and to set up on reformed principles a
Church more absolute by the unity of
its members in its authority over the
world than the Papacy was even in its
palmiest days. Looked at politically, how-
ver, we cannot see that this is desirable;
indeed, if we view it in the light of past
history it is difficult to regard it otherwise
than as most undesirable. Power, like every-
thing else, is evil in its excess, and the expe-
rience of all countries and creeds throughout
all time shows that spiritual power intoxicates
soonest, and whilst it operates produces the
most lasting and mischievous effects. Poli-
tically speaking, it is the interest of the world
to have divided, not united churches—suffi-
ciently divided to neutralise ecclesiastical
persecution, but sufficiently united. on common
grounds of charity to lead to common action
for the common good. Wherever any one sect,
or two sects, predominate there are painful
sectarian rivalries, or an injurious interference
with the action of the State, which wastes its
energy and retards its action. But where, as
in England, freedom of thought has produced
numerous bodies, each interpreting the
general truth in a particular way, the political
necessity for charitable toleration secures that
liberty of the individual, that thorough inde-

pendenoe in religious freedom, which is
sanctified by time, and in the end becomes
the nation's best safeguard even for the main-
tenance of its political liberty.
There is, therefore, no reason why we

should not wish Dr. Dorzweam well in the
formation of his Old Catholic Party, as a
resisting power to Papal oppression, but so far
as unity with other gommuaions is concerned,
we have no desiro to see such a thing effected.

To fight and conquer liberty of thought and

i
action s one thing; to unite with the view of
forming a huge corporation which might
become dangerous, is quite another matter,
and, in obedience to the warnings of history,
We prefer failure to success in this well-
meant effort on the part of the old Catholics of
Germany.

articles.title: REPUBLIC OF FRANCE.
articles.text:
THE REPUBLIC OF FRANCE.

A GOVERNMENT like that of M. Dims' in
France must always be on the edge of peril,
unless, indeed, it really conform itself to the
principles which it proposes for its basis. It
cannot serve two masters; and GOD and
Mammon are not wider apart than the Rurals
and the Republicans. At present, the Dag-
DENT shows himself fraithAtl to the Republic,

and, in his personal bearing, is not a very bad
copy of the WASHINGTON model. Yet, ho
now inhabits a palace, on the principle, how-
ever, that a house is better occupied than
left empty, and with the excuse, were one
needed, that his own dwelling was destroyed
and has not yet been restored. But indeed,
as chief magistrate of the nation, he deserves,
while faithful, to be lodged in national
quarters. Still, by using the qualification of
"Conservative Republic," he fails, on the one
hand, to secure the implicit confidence of the
Republican party, while, on the other hand,
by adhering to the Republic under any
epithet, he excites the distrust of those who
cannot divest themselves of the prepossession
for kingship.
The prohibition of the GI.IIBETTA banquet,
even, will not get rid of that distrust; instead
of which, unless the disappointed party exer-
cise great forbearance, it is adapted to impede
that union of all shades of opinion and senti-
ment adverse to monarchy which is necessary
to establish on firm foundations any Republic,
call it by what epithet you will. The most
formidable rival of M. Tirrtats, however, is a
man sufficiently versatile and self-command-
ing, to bear so palpable a snubbing with a
politic equanimity; in which case, it may
yield him more and better capital than any ho
could have made by ever so stirring a speech
to a gathering of supporteri ever so enthusi-
astic. The series of levtses at his hotel which
were substituted for the prohibited festivity,
joined to the weakness shown in prohibiting it
at all, and to the obvious indecency of delaying
the interdict till the appointed hour of dining,
will do for M. GAMBETTA and his immediate
friends as much as, or more than the most
successful festival without molestation of any
kind could have accomplished.
M. Timms cannot, on reflection, be sur-
prised, or complain that M. GAMBETTA com-
mented upon the act of the Prefect of SAVOY
as he did. He had a perfect right to adduce
it as one proof of dislike to the Republic. In
fact, ho might with reason have said more.
But ho had the adroitness to leave open a door
of escape for the PItI7.SIDENT, by attributing
the manifestation to only "some of those who
govern France." Whether M. Timms was a
party to the interference or not, nobody can
doubt the prudence, as nobody has a right to
question the sincerity of the other comments
made by M. GAMBETTA. on the occasion. Re-
publicans, however, should of all thing 5, he
observed, be careful to obey the law. Let
them but show a little political sagacity, and
the destinies of France were in their hands.
The origin of the three Republics, was, on
comparison, in favour of that now existing.
He loft the first to condemn itself by its own
bloody history. In 1848 everyone acclaimed
the Republic; the majority, nevertheless,
meaning all the time to destroy it as soon as
possible. Now, the Republic, at first un-
popular, was slowly but surely gaining
ground; and every genuine Republican must
aid the cause by a sound discretion and perfect
respect for the law. Nothing could be more
admirable.

Remembering how devoted a friend M.
TRIERS was supposed:to. be to the House of
Orleans, and the inveteracy of political pre-
judice natural to
.the mind of an aged.
politician, M. GAMBETTA is in ;the right to
hasten slowly. If, at some future day,
he be destined to occupy the yachted
place, it will be all the easier for him when
entanglements have been removed and diffi-
culties have been smoothed away, by means to
which it would hardly have suited either his
temperament or his policy to have had re-
course. It would not, for example, have
pleased Ai. GAMRETTA so much as it seems to
have gratified M. TRIERS to receive from the
Russian AMBASSADOR in Paris, immediately on
his return to France, an assurance sent by the
CZAR that the meeting of the three EMPERORS
in Berlin boded nothing against the Republic,
especially on the side of Russia, Yet the
experience of America has shown that a
Republic may place some dependence oven
upon the word of the Autocrat of the North.
We are not more disposed to accept without
abatement M. ABOUT'S version of the matter of
his temporary arrest by the German authorities
in Alsace, tb.an we are to excuse tho injustice

or extenuate the folly of that ill-judged
measure; and the retirement from Versailles
in disgust of COUNT Amin is a fable already
falsified by a practical contradiction. The
SITYLOCK of PRUSSIA may insist upon his
pound of political flesh; but even he need not
be supposed anxious for shedding a drop of
blood more. The tendency to government
according to a freely spoken public opinion',
which has certainly shown itself in two of the
Imperial States of Europe, may, after all,
influence the third, notwithstanding its in-
veterate despotism, its remote situation, its
semi-barbarism, and its wide distribution.

We expect that the PRESIDENT Of the RE-
PUBLIC, having in view the extremely attenu-
ated. state of that thread of life which the
fabled sisters will one day find so yielding to
their scissors, is quite engrossed by certain
things which he would like to see made facts
before the thread:, is out in two. He would
naturally like to see what remains of the soil
of Franco free from foreign presence ; and he
hopes to achieve that series of financial opera-
tions which will accomplish the desired result.
The matter of delicacy as between himself and
the free traders of France, and between France
and foreign States, particularly England, re-
quires management; but managing is in his
way, and. he evidently hopes to succeed. For
the rest he also has an edifice to crown, and
he seems to hope for success in such measures
as the appointment of a VICE-PRESIDENT, an
upper Chamber of Legislature, and a new
electoral law for either the one representative
chamber, or for the two. The existence of a
SENATE in the United. States keeps one of his
reputed thoughts within a tone of a Republic,
whether called " Conservative " or not. The law
by which a successor to the so-called National
Assembly shall be chosen must be judged of
when we know what is to be proposed. As for
the nomination of a VICE-PRESIDENT, neither
M. Timms nor the Assembly is likely to pitch
upon 11L GAMBETTS. But that will not
eventually settle the matter. The Vice will
naturally take the place of the Principal when:
he vacates the chair; but who shall be elected.
Chief in his stead, that will be the question.

articles.title: COLONEL NORTH AND MR. BENYON.
articles.text:
COLONEL NORTH AND MR. BENYON.

WHEN we read what our daily contem-
poraries think proper to publish of the ad-
dresses of Mr. ARCH and his follow agitators,
we generally find very candid, very moderate,
and very fair views of the situation taken as
between the farmer and labourer, some kind of
appreciation of facts as they exist, accom-
panied by suggestions as to the best way of
altering them where they need alteration in
the interest of the parties concerned. Of
course any statement they may make as to the
amount of wages paid to the labourer, or as to
the state of his dwelling, cannot apply to every
ease, as over such a wide field there must be
differences which no general statement can
fairly cover, But on the whole the labourers,
and those who have spoken for them, have
delivered themselves like men, having some
reliance on truth, and some belief in justice.
When we turn from these, however, to
certain members of Parliament deliver-
ing themselves at agricultural meetings
a strange contrast is perceived. Such men
as Colonel NORTH and Mr. BENTON talk
as if they had just been wakened up after a
sleep of half a century. They are either
greatly before their time or greatly behind it.
Clearly they are not mentally in it. They deal
with the affairs of their parishes and counties
as if they were playing the parts of benevolent
old men at the Lyceum or the Adolphi
theatres. They deplore the ingratitude of the
labourers as a most iniquitous and unnatural
thing—too bad to find place in their hearts,
had it not been put there by malignant "agi-
tators ;" whilst Colonel NORTH, with evident
huskiness of throat, advises the farmers not to
punish them—the labourers—for this, but to
take them to their arms again as brothers,
give them their old kindly eleven shillings a
week, we presume, and their ordinary allow-
ance of skimmed milk. We shall have some day,
soon, no: doubt, a great meeting of farmers and
labourers in Oxfordshire, when at the word of
command from Colonel NORTH they will rush
into each others' arms to the sound of joyous
music, and Mr. Anal will as a finish be burned
i# effigy by BoDrisita who in sight of tho

whole assembly will grasp the hand of the
farmer who flogged him, and kiss the whip
with which his well-deserved punishment was
administered.

Are we to laugh or look grave when we read
such speeches as those of Colonel NORTH and
Mr. BENYON ? Will they carry the farmers
and labourers back into the golden age, or will
they redden our winter skies with the glare of
incendiary fires? Are we to have repetition
after repetition of half-idiotic gabble about
"agitators," or the serious and sensible talk
of men not irredeemably committed to folly,
like Colonel NORIII and others of his political
calibre? There is a song singing itself in the
ears of the peasantry, which has a maddening
chorus, chanted by hungry children at home,
and this is its burden—

The landlord's rents at Christmas came,
His fields and woods wore crammed with game;
The farmers' barns with wheat,
The parson had his glebe and tithe,
While they who held the plough and scythe
Must beg or steal to eat,

With great seriousness it may be asked
whether or not such persons as the Noun's
and the BENYONS ought to be shut up, or be
compelled to keep silence in the presence of
dangers they have not the vision to see, or
the sense to understand? Can anything come
from such a way of dealing with such a ques-
tion but mischief? Has it not been sufficiently
acknowledged that the position of the English
peasant is bad, and ought to be made better?
And is it not sickening, after such an acknow-
ledgment, that such men as we have men-
tioned should be permitted to chatter a pro-
voking gibberish, which, like children playing
with fire, may unexpectedly set the house in
a blaze.

articles.title: ANTI-PAPAL MOVEMENT.
articles.text:
THE ANTI-PAPAL MOVEMENT.

IP we refer to the proceedings of the "Old
Catholics" in Germany, and to other symptoms
of motive antipathy between religious factions
in Europe, it is not with any view to weigh either
the ecclesiastical or the theological importance
of the fads and o f their possible issues, so much as
to report progress on the altering phases of
public opinion. The general cause of national
freedom has much at stake in the upshot. We
cannot, for example, but sympathise with the
men of Antwerp in their celebration of the
overthrow even in a single city of that" priestly
influence" which has swayed their local
government for ten years, but will now sway it no
longer. The little constitutional Kingdom of
Belgium has had hard work of it; for nowhere
else are the priests more persevering or more
crafty; but, under the presidency of a father
and a son faithful to their undertakings, and
with a burgher population who will not be
priestrld, the Liberal party has hitherto been
able to preserve its own. Switzerland too,
republic as she is, contains so many Roman
Catholics, and consequently so many priests
that she also can:afford neither to intermit her
vigilance nor to relax her hold. An ecclesiastic,
calling himself Bishop of HEBRON, in the
Holy Land! has been trying to give the
authorities trouble. Had the Council of State
of the Canton of Geneva " tendorhanded
touched the nettle," it would have " stung
them for their pains ; " but that authority has
"seized it like a man of mettle," though we
are not sure, such is the nettle nature in priests,
that "it soft as silk 'remains." Be this as it
may the Council has forbidden him to exercise
his episcopal functions anywhere in Swiss
territory; and it remains for the POPE and
himself to determine whether he shall transfer
them to the city in Palestine from which he
takes his title. As the Cantonal authorities
first took the advice, and obtained the consent
of the Federal Council of Berne, we may
expect that MEM/MOD'S menace to continue
bishoping it in spite of them, will be met as
becomes a popular government threatened by
an emissary of the POPE.
By the way, this bishop question is the very
point at which things have arrived in Germany.
If Roman Catholic Prelates have no more
sense of modesty, or art in affeetation of that
Virtue, than to flourish their Boman appoint-
ment in the face of Empires, Kingdoms, and
Republics, they must expect to be treated with
much less ceremony than Q. • (Ix supercilious-
ness seems to claim, The speciality of the
anti-Papal movement in Gtermarty, however,

is its twofold character. Not merely does
Prince BISMAJICK, as Chancellor of the Empire,
send away the Jesuits, but a largo body of the
clergy and the laity themselves, calling them-
selves "Old Catholics," rise up against the
universal Head of their own Church, and,
utterly repudiating the " infallibility " and
consequent plenary authority which, on the
strength of a pretendedly general council, he
asserts and claims, they resolve to be their
own masters and to govern themselves as a
religious body according to such rules and
regulations as by common consent duly
obtained they may choose to adopt. They will
be a free church, and perhaps in a free State.
This is, in brief, the meaning and purpose
of the Old Catholic Congress of four hundred
deputies, held from day to day last week at
Cologne. All of them seem to be quite agreed
in such principles as follow—ecclesiastical
freedom, perfect tolerance, Christian unity
with other churches, freedom of marriage,
government by an electoral assembly con-
sisting of clergymen and laymen, and, above
all, the election of bishops by a committee of
seven persons, the majority, as we understand ,
it, being laymen, or, at least, non-theologians.
Under these general principles and provisions,
numerous reforms upon the old state of things
are in contemplation.
Independence of the Vatican is strongly
asserted in one of the resolutions. " Those
priests,' it runs, "who have been suspended
or excommunioated because of their fidelity to
their religion, are qualified to exercise all
pastoral functions; not only can they validly
administer the means of grace employed by
the Church, but they arc permitted so to do in
consideration of the conditions of our need
caused by the Vatican Bishops and clergy,
and, in eases of necessity, must consider
themselves as bound to administer them."
These being the very words of a resolution
passed at the Bavarian Congress, a year ago,
show the progress opinion is making among
the most Catholic of the Catholics in Ger-
many.

On the subject of differences of creed, the
resolution adopted is as follows :—" The Con-
gress reiterates the expression of hope for a
reunion of the now divided Christian Confes-
sions, as contained in the Munich programmes
of Whitsuntide and September, 1871. It ex-
presses the wish that the theologians of all
Confessions may direct their attention to this
point, and elects a Committee to which the
commission is given-1. To put itself in com-
munication with the already existing (or those
lin course of formation) seeieties for the re-
moval of churchly schism. 2. To make and
induce seiantifio examination, in regard to the
existing differences, and to show the possi-
bility of their removal; and to promote the
publication of the results of these examina-
tions in theological scientific works and
journals. 3. To promote by means of popular
writings and essays the knowledge of the doc-
trines, usages, and condition of the separated
churches and confessions; the proper appre-
ciation of the existing points of unity and
difference, and to awaken and to maintain in
wider circles the understanding of, and inte-
rest in, this desirable approach."
We make no pretension to weigh the im-
portance of this groat movement in a suffi-
ciently well adjusted balance;. but no special
Perspicacity is needed to assure one's self of its
momentous character. There were present on
the occasion divines of many creeds, and of
many countries; and, among the rest, such
men as the Bishops of ELY and LINCOLN, and
the Dean of WESTMINSTER. Archbishop
MiNtinget has had a distant, yet keen eye
upon the whole proceeding, and has much to
say about the difficulty of conceiving how
Bishop WORDSWORTH and Dean STANLEY can
have come together, or how they can possibly
agree now that they have met under one roof.
The obvious answer is that the Church of
England has not more or greater differences
than the Church of Item° has had, and has
still ; and there is another answer better still,
that men may, of their own accord, agree to
differ whom no compulsion, ecclesiastical or
civil, could ever constrain to see and judge
alike. At any rate, if ecclesiastics and theo-
logians cannot agree in all matters of either
opinion or practice, their renunciation of a

foreign yoke and determination to judge and
provide for themselves arc excellent things on
their own account, and aro full of promise to
peoples who see in the mere tools of a foreign
dictator sending his emissaries into all coun-
tries the greatest enemies to national freedom
and family peace.

We shall not be understood as entirely
approving of the manner in which Prince
Btalikudic deals with the Ultramontane
churchmen who strove to thwart his purposes.
But he may be viewed as compelled by circum-
stances to canform himself gradually to
enlightened opinion in Germany. There is no
mistaking now which way that tends, even
among the Catholics themselves. Take, how-
ever, a yet better example,—Dr. EWALD, than
whom there is no greater name among scholars
and thinkers in the Fatherland, and who
represents Hanover in its Imperial Parliament.
He thinks that religious freedom has been
hindered rather than advanced by the CsA.N-
cELLon's policy ; but why ? Because he
regards it, in reference to the Jesuits, as pro-
ceeding upon the principle of rooting up errors
by main force. Now, we cannot doubt the
truth of what the learned professor says,
when he affirms that Englishmen cannot
derive an accurate notice of the state of German
thought from German, newspapers, "owing,"
as he adds, "to the want of freedom of the
press." Nevertheless, we are quite prepared to
believe from what we do really see, that public
opinion is even more Liberal than it appears to
be, Thus we are strengthened in the persua-
sion, that BISAURCK, so long as he continues at
the helm of affairs, and any minister who
may come after him, will be obliged to act
more and more upon a really Liberal policy.
At the same time it can never be tolerated by
any State, Republican or Monarchical, that
respects itself, be it Switzerland or Germany,
that men who disclaim allegiance to it to begin
with, shall set its laws at defiance, and
practise against its independent interests, with
perfect impunity. But a further light will be
thrown upon the practical question in Ger-
many, when the Prussian Diet, in its approach-
ing session shall be called upon to secure by
logialativo meroures the bU vereiguLy of the State
in matters concerning all civil life, against all
doubts, reservations, and encroachments on the j
part of the Church.

articles.title: DESTRUCTIVE WEATHER IN THE NORTH.
articles.text:
DESTRUCTIVE WEATHER IN THE
NORTH.

WE regret to learn that there is a sad pro-
speot of suffering in the North of Scotland and
of Ireland. In the former, there have been
successive storms of snow, earlier and
heavier than have been known in the same
latitude for many a year; accompanied, as is
natural, by keen and cutting Northern blasts.
Much of the grain crops is untouched by the
sickle, and what had been reaped remained
out in stook. The farmers, especially the
small farmers, must, therefore, suffer severely.
Parts of Aberdeenshire seemed to be exempt ;
but only from snow. After three weeks' rain
on that side, there came on ;Wednesday in
this week a perfect deluge, by which, besides
the damage done by the flood along the line of
the rivers and of the city of Aberdeen, the
httrvest, it is stated, is "irretrievably ruined."
The state of things is similar in Ulster, where
the Moderator of the Presbyterian Church,
the first religious body in the province, has
issued an address to the ministers, in reference
to the continuous rains and the distressing
state of the crops, requesting that upon Sunday
next, the 29th inst., they will bring the matter
before their congregations, and call upon their
people to engage in earnest prayer that GOD
may avert his judgment, and save the country
from want and famine.

articles.title: LABOUR, REPRESENTATION
articles.text:
THE LABOUR, REPRESENTATION

LEAGUE.

At a meeting of the Labour Representation
League, held at Coekspur-street, Charing Cross,
the following resolution, moved by Mr. R. Marsden
Latham, the president, seconded by Mr. Henry
Broadhurst, and supported by Messrs. Paterson,
Campin, Applegarth, Ecearius, Savage, Motters-
head, and Brighty, was adopted unanimously
"That the Labour Representation League having
repeatedly, by reso'ution and otherwise, urged the
settlement of the Alabama dispute by arbitration,
feels bound to express its approval of the Goner

SEPT. 28, 1872.

raward, without, however, expressing any opinioa
as to the equity of the amount awarded in a
merely commercial point of view. This League
feels that the great object to be aimed at by the
Governments of both countries is friendliness of
relationship between two peoples mutually pledged
by ties of kindred to amity and peace, and it
views with unmixed satisfaction a settlement
which leaves England and America, as they ought
to be, side by side in promoting the advancement
of industry and civilisation throughout the world."
At a special meeting of the officers of the League,
held on Monday at their offices in Cockspur-streett
Charing-cross, Mr. R. M, Latham, the presidenh,
in the chair, the action of the ballot at Preaten
election was discussed, and the conduct of the
Conservatives in systematically frustrating the
intention of the Act, by the collection of tickets
from electors immediately after polling, severely
censured. Surprise was expressed that "One of
the great political parties of the State, calling
itself 'Constitutional,' and represented at the
Preston election by Mr. Gorst, its chief electioneer-
ing manager, should have set the example of
seeking to effect a subversion of the law by its
erasion." It was agreed that the working classes
in Preston should be at once communicated with,
in order to obtain precise particulars as to the
alleged violation of the spirit of the Ballot Act,
prelimary to a general meeting of the League,
which was convened for Friday, to determine
what steps can be taken for preventing the recur-
rence in the future of such tactics, and for secur-
ing the free and untramelled exercise of the
franchise.

MR. BROADHURST AND TIM MASONS.
It has been decided by the stonemasons of
London to recognise the services of Mr. Broad-
hurst, which he rendered to the masons during
the last lock-out in the building trades, by a testi-
monial. At a general meeting held at Wileocke's
Rooms on the 13th of September, 1872, the follow-
ing resolution was carried unanimously :

That, in consideration of the energy and practical
ability with which Brother Broadhurst has con-
ducted the business connected with the late dispute,
now so happily and advantageously. terminated—
this meeting is of opinion that he is worthy of A
testimonial.

The following committee were elected to carry
out the above object :—Wm. Walpole, Southwark
Lodge; Chas. Bray, South London Lodge; John
McPherson, Southwark Lodge; Daniel McKay,
West London Lodge; Wm. Bowman, South
London Lodge; Henry Jones, Battersea Lodge;
John Stewart, Pavior's Arms; T. Spencer, Shore
ditch Lodge; Henry Nisbet, chairman; Thomas
Badwin, secretary; Jobn Banks, treasurer. Thq
committee will meet at the Sun Inn, Mason-street,
to rec9ive subscriptions, on the following dates,
September 28th, October sth and 12th, from 6 to
9 p.m.
It has not yet been decided what form the testi-
monial shall take, but we trust that a liberal
response will be given to the committee's appeal.

CLOSING OF PUBLIC HOUSES.
The Licensing Committee of the Liverpool
magistrates, at the sessions held on Thursdays
decided to give another turn to the screw in regard
to the hours of closing. They came to the reso-
lution to close all licensed houses on Sunday nights
at nine o'clock. The hours on week days are to
be from seven o'clock in the morning to eleven et
night. An attempt was made to induce the
magistrates to fix ten o'clock as the closing hour;
but it failed. If the new regulations are found to
work in Liverpool, with its vast and varied popu-
lation—and especially on Sundays—the result will
be surprising. We observe that in London ft
number of publicans in the neighbourhood of
theatres and music halls have received permission
to keep their houses open until one o'clock in the
morning for the benefit of persons professionailY
engaged in the theatres and the audiences attend-
ing the same. How the publicans are to decide
whether customers who present themselves after
midnight have or have not been to a theatre is not
known.

A. civil service class has also been formed to

THIRD-CLASS RAILWAY FARES

_
The experiment—for such it confessedly is—of
attaching third-class carriages to fast trains, has,
in the main, had the effect of largely increasing
the passenger traffic; the only instance of com-
plaint has been that made by the chairman of the
Great Western, who inferentially declared the
third-class passengers had been carried at a loss.
But upon this point he is at issue with the other
great railways of the kingdom—the North-
Western, the Midland, the Great Northern,
South-Eastern, South-Western, of which
show increased traffic and augmented receipts.
The chairman of each have successively declared
that the true policy is to endeavour to accommo-
date the masses—a sentiment which we most
cordially endorse. The railway companies are,
even as at present existing, great monopolies ;
they have exceptional powers in the way ot
closing thoroughfares and diverting traffic, and
they ought, in compensation, to servo the public,
for whose professed benefit those exceptional
powers were given, in the best possible manner.
On the part of the railways, it is contended that
the increase in the receipts is not so largo as would
have been the case had the companies not generously
given the masses the boon of third-class tickets by
fast trains. To this there are many answers.

Primarily, the experiment has only been a short
time in operation, and has not yet had a fair trial.
But we confess we have little sympathy with the
complaining parties. The Great Western pays
61 per cent., the Midland 7 per cent., the North-
Western pays 7i per cent., the South-Eastern 3}
per cent., and so on through the whole category,
and we are at a loss to conceive whence the
complaint arises. The fact is that the railways
have participated in the general prosperity of the
country; but we question whether they have done
so to the extent they might have. True, they
have lost a few second-class passengers, but this
only proves a case against themselves, viz., that
hitherto they had not been meeting the wants of
the travelling public for cheap accommodation.
Those who knew Mr. Hudson, "the Railway
King," know that in his retirement he constantly
said that the policy of the railway companies
generally had been a great mistake. They had
run trains at long distances at high fares, whereas
they ought to have run trains at cheap fares for
short journeys in order to develop the traffic.
At last it seems the companies are about to
carry out the purposes for which they were
established and their monopolies granted, that of
affording travelling facilities to the public; and if
for the moment the profits are not so great as they
expected, there can be no doubt that those who
have adopted this wise policy will in the long run
be the gainers. We confess to the smallest
amount of sympathy with those who complain
when receiving a 7 per cent. dividend.—lnvest-
ment Review.

articles.title: INDUSTRIAL CLASSES IN FOREIGN COUNTRIES.
articles.text:
INDUSTRIAL CLASSES IN FOREIGN
COUNTRIES.

Further reports from her Majesty's diplomatic
and consular agents abroad respecting the condition
of the industrial classes have just been issued by
the Foreign Office. Amon); them arc reports from
Consul Donohoe, Baltimore, and Consul-General
Archibald, New York. The former says that the
price of unimproved land in Maryland ranges
from 16s. to £6 per acre. "Most of this land has
been at some time under cultivation, but has been
allowed to run to waste upon the abolition of
slavery. The practice of ranting farms prevails
very generally throughout this State. The usual
method is renting on shares—that is to say, the
owner accepts in lieu of rent from one-third to
one-half the crop, the tenant in most cases pro-
viding everything necessary for the working of
the farm. In a few cases the owner furnishes seeds,
implements, and stock, and receives two-thirds of
the crop." Ho considers the Western States offer
much bettor prospects for immigrants, and states that
food is on the whole cheaper than in England, but
clothing is much dearer. Ho thus concludes :
"A respectable artizan coming to the United
States and bringing up his family here has every
chance, with the excellent free education he can
bestow upon his children, of seeing them rise to
pAtionsthey never would attain in England, and,
as a wneral thing, a steady and sober mechanic
will have a better position and more money to
spend on comforts than he would have in a like
position at home. I could cite many cases of
the prospority of omigrant4rom the United Xing.

dom in the United States, but will give only one,
with which lam well acquainted. The son of a
tenant of four acres upon the estate of a noble-
man in Ireland emigrated to the United States about
the year 1848. At first he worked as a labourer
in an iron foundry. In 1852 he was a working
gardener on wages of £6 per month. In 1870 he
transmitted to Ireland enough money to purchase
his landlord's castle, then for sale, and at the
same time owned in the United States a sugar

plantation upon which he had spent about
£40,000; also a very fine firm and valuable fancy
stock, as well as a handsome town residence. He
came very nearly being elected United States
Senator. I doubt very rauch if he had remained
in Ireland he would even have had the chance of
being a Poor-law Guardian. I know another
case of an emigrant from a British possession who
cannot oven write his own name, and who, by
steady industry, perseverance, is now worth over
£20,000, lie is not a penurious man, but gene-
rous and charitable to a high degree. Many
such examples as the above could, of course, be
given from our colonies, but it is a matter for
the consideration of the British mechanic whether
as long as he had steady employment at home, he
had better relinquish it and seek his fortune in a
foreign land, far away from all his kin."

THE FIRST ARTISAN MEMBER OF THE

CANADIAN PARLIAMENT.

The Daily Witness of Montreal publishes a
portrait and memoir of Mr. 11. B. Witton, the
first working man elected to a seat in the Canadian
Parliament. The Witness says :—Henry Buck-
ingham Witton, M.P. for Hamilton, was born at
the small village of South Lopham, Norfolk, Eng.
land, October 21, 1831, and is now forty-one
years of age. At Diss Mr. Witton received such
education, very imperfect and rudimentary, as his
parents, who were poor, could with much difficulty
and many sacrifices of their own comfort, afford
to give him. Here also he was apprenticed to the
trade of coachmaking, but in consequence of the
discontinuance of this business by his employer,
he was thrown on his own resources at the early
age of seventeen. His subsequent employments
were in Thetford, London, and Manchester.
There Mr. Witton was attracted into fields of
usefulness, and became a worker in the cause of
education and other much-needed reforms, many
of which have now happily been accomplished.
In 1853 he emigrated to the United States, and
for throe years remained a resident of Troy, N.Y.
In 1856 he removed to Hamilton, Canada, where
he has resided ever since, and for nearly the whole
period has boon in the service of the Great
Western Railway. For some years past he has
been foreman in the paintshop of that Company,
and has performed his work faithfully and
well. On his first appointment the Company
profited largely by economies:introduced by him
During all the years of his working life he has
been gradually improving his originally scanty
education. After coming to Hamilton, he
acquired French and Latin, and applied himself
with enthusiasm to the study of practical geology,
astronomy, and microscopy, to the latter of which
especially he has for several years devoted most
of his leisure time. His reading, however, has
not been exclusively scientific, but varied and
catholic, and his knowledge of general literature,
history, politics, and political economy, makes
him an agreeable companion for those who care
for neither the mysteries of the stars nor the
marvels of the ponds. His life has been essen-
tially a quiet one, spent in work and study. He
has in a larger degree than most men commanded
the respect and confidence of his follow-workmen,
and many votes were cast for him and his ticket
during the late election on grounds purely per-
sonal to himself. He is moderate and courteous
in speech, and has passed through a severe
election contest with the goodwill of all parties.

articles.title: GEORGE FRANCIS TRAIN ON COMIC SONGS AND FREE LOVE.
articles.text:
GEORGE FRANCIS TRAIN ON COMIC
SONGS AND FREE LOVE.

George Francis Train is a. t present in San
Francisco, and the Californian Evening
Republican sent a reporter to interview him.
While our reporter (says the Republican), was
looking over these things, a short, stubby,
rather pleasant looking middle-aged gentle-
man, dressed in a grey cheviot, entered the
room. Train saw him, and the two rushed
into each other's arms. "Train ? "
" Massett I ' were the only words they uttered,
till their hold of each other relaxed. Pipes
exclaimed, "My dear fellow!" and Train
replied, "How are you, old boy ?" We never
thought Train had so much weakness as lie
exhibited, while gazing into the blue eyes and
at the unkempt hair of Pipes. The greetings
of the old friends over, Pipes, brushing his
grey locks from his forehead with his right
hand, and seizing Train by the arm with his
left, and, assuming a highly tragic mien and

voice, exclaimed, "Train, I have a favour to
beg of you—a favour I beg of you to grant—
for our old friendship's sake." What is it F"
exclaimed Train—who acted as if he suspected
Pipes's reason had been unseated from its
throne. " What can Ido for you ? " "Well,
let me my tale unfold," slowly mumbled
Pipes. " I have made a hit—a decided
hit." "Hit what? Who? When?" ex-
claimed Train, who began to get impatient.
"I have written 'Open the Door,' the most
popular song of the day, and if I could only
get you to sing it to-night my fortune would
be, made, because a song sung by Train would
be more valuable than the largest diamond in
Harpending's mine in Arizona." "Are you
mad ?" exclaimed Train. "Me, a candidate
for President of the United States, sing a song.
Why, what do you take me for? I wouldn't
sing a song for a million dollars" "But
'Open the Door,'" said Pipes, "is —"
"Open the Door, be d—d," exclaimed Train.
"I am no wandering troubador, to be hired to
sing anybody's songs. I am the great Re-
former of the age—the man of destiny, and
the future President of the United States, and
don't talk to me about singing." Train was
evidently mad, and poor Pipes stood like one
entranced. Just then a waiter entered with a
tiny pink card, which smelled so strongly of
pachouly as to give a pleasant odour over
the whole apartment. All the hard lines
in Train's face relaxed as he stood gaz-
ing at the little morsel of pasteboard.
Stepping outside the door, Train imme-
diately returned, accompanied by an elegantly-
attired lady of majestic demeanour and most
voluptuous beauty. She was nearly as tall as
Train' and quite as stout, with a complexion
of that brilliant brunette so rare and withal
so charming. Her hair was darker than the
raven's plumage; her eyes, large, full, and
oval, were so intensely black that they seemed
to repel the light of day; her mouth was
clothed ;with the most bewitching of smiles.
Altogether, she was a most beautiful woman.
Miss R. F. Mli.—the lady's name—apologised
for intruding on Train's time, and excused
herself by stating that she called to see him
because she - thought he—like herself—was
aiming to liberetb—Women from the thraldom
of men. For liehelf, she thought marriage
was more disirliCeTal than open prostitution.
That every woman had-a natural right to select
the father of hot. Children. "Madam,'' said
Train, interrupting her, "I, it is true, desire
to elevate women in the social scale, and make
her the equal of man in every respect; but I
cannot subscribe to the ideas you have ex-
pressed. On the contrary, I consider the institu-
tion of marriage one of the most sacred,
which should not be severed except by death,
or unfaithfulness. I wish you to distinctly
understand, madam, that I do not endorse the
Woodhull free-love heresy. I advocate
women's rights for the purpose of strengthen-
ing her hold on man's love,
,not to bring her
into his contempt. I have read a circular, of
which I believe you, madam, are the author."
"Have you ? " inquired the lady, "and now,
pray, Mr. Train, give inc your honest opinion
about it." "Well, I can't trim, and wouldn't
if I could. I will tell you what I think of the
circular. I consider it a disgrace to woman to
pen such sensual, unwomanly ideas, and more
disgraceful still in her to circulate such moral
poison among the homes of the virtuous women
of' America.' "Mr. Train," exclaimed the
lady, rising from her seat, and looking at Train
as if she would wither him at a glance. "Do
not be angry, madam," replied Train, "I slid
not desire to give offence. You asked me to
express my honest opinion. I have only done
as you asked, and, pray excuse me for
saying further, that your own action
in getting angry at the expression
of an opinion evoked by yourself—is a proof
that your assumption of the character of
moral reformer is a disguise." "Sir l " she
exclaimed bepeath her teeth, her face almost
white with rage. " You see, madam, that I
never get mad at what they say about me,
though a servile press and the hirelings of
monopoly and corruption have been hounding
and abusing me for years. Ido not get mad.
The work I am destined to accomplish keeps
me above that weakness of human nature
which make us angry- at whatever displeases
us." The lady sat down, drew a deep sigh,
and remarked :—" Well, perhaps you're right
about the human weakness, but you are
decidedly wrong about my work on free love.
I think it is the cruelest of tyranny to compel
a woman to endure the embraces of a man she
does not love." Just at this instant about a
dozen gentlemen came in. After they were
seated Train invited the lady to proceed with
her tale of love, but she declined, remarking
that she was disappointed at her reception,
that she had expected to have been met with
outstretched arms, with warmth and ardour,
instead of with icy coldness and a puritanical
sermon on chastity, and she swept out of the
room in a manner which showed that she was
not well pleased.

A publican in the Gray's Inn-road, Thomas
William Walton by name, has been eonvisted
of setting fire to his houee while his family
were asleep in it; and the sentence passed
on him in the Central Criminal Court is ten
years' penal servitude,

articles.title: LATEST INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.

The number of visitors admitted to the In-
ternational Exhibition on Wednesday was by
season tickets, 360; on payment of 2s. 6d.,
1,072; total, 1,438.

A deputation from Newcastle on Wednesday
waited upon the Inland Revenue Commis-
sioners in respect to a mitigation of fifty heavy
fines imposed upon licensed victuallers for
selling beer and spirits on the Newcastle Town
Moor on the Sunday previous to the last New-
castle race week.

The King of Denmark is seriously indisposed,
and has kept his bed for . some days. His
medical attendants have recommended com-
plete repose for some time.
The three men who were originally charged
with killing the lad Finn in Eaton-square
were on Wednesday again brought up at the
Westminster Police-court. A coroner's war-
rant had been granted against two of them,
but the jury exonerated the third man, who
was accordingly discharged, but the other two
were remanded for the medical testimony.

A Reuter's telegram from Paris says that
the Duke of Edinburgh and Prince Arthur
arrived there yesterday, and immediately left
again for Baden-Baden, in order to be present
at the obsequies of the Princess Feodora
Hohenlohe-Langenburg, sister of her Majesty
the Queen.

A show of cheese and butter under the
auspices of the Frotne District Agricultural
Society was held on Wednesday. Prizes of
the value of upwards of £2OO were awarded
for the produce of some of the best dairies of
Somerset, Wilts, Dorset, and Ireland. About
140 tons, principally prime Cheddars, were
pitched for sale' and good prices realised, 725.
to 80s. being the top figures.

The Manchester Chamber of Commerce on
Wednesday passed a resolution concurring
in the opinion of the Select Parliamentary
Committee of last session that waterways
should not be absorbed by railways, and ex-
pressed its opinion that the transfer of the
canals between Manchester and Liverpool to
certain railway directors would be adverse to
the commercial interests of the two towns.

A man named Henry Cripps, a Protestant,
employed as foreman by Messrs. Smith and
Smyths, flour ',merchants, Drogheda, has re-
ceived. a lettor threatening him with death.

The steamer Garland, which arrived at
Greenock last night, reports having experi-
enced on the passage from Londonderry
most terrific gale from the north-north-east.
The vessel lost her life boat, and the waves
carried away several stanchions. To save his
vessel the captain had to throw overboard at
an early hour of the morning 1.50 head of
cattle.

The 0/asgots Mail states that a young man
in the employment of a firm in the northern
district of that city went into a bank to draw
some money, and it is alleged, was overpaid
£lOO in £5 notes. Information was given to
the police, and the party accused was taken
into custody, pending inquiries. Search was
made for the notes, but they have not been
recovered.

A heavy thunderstorm broke over Jersey
on Wednesday morning, which was followed
by a violent storm of hail and sleet. Heavy
rain preceded the thuuder.
The price of coal has been reduced at Great
Yarmouth 4s, per ton.

The ex-Emperor and Empress of the French
are expected to leave Cowes for Chiselhurst
to-day (Saturday). His Imperial Majesty's
health has much improved during his stay
in the Isle of Wight.
A second general meeting of the creditors
of Mr. F. Strange, the proprietor of the Surrey
Zoological Gardens, whose affairs are under
liquidation, was held on Wednesday at the
Manor House, Walworth, when the creditors
present confirmed the resolutions passed at
the first general meeting (subject to the
admission of certain disputed claims),
accepting a composition of is. in the pound,
and appointing Mr. Sydney Smith public
accountant, and a creditor trustee.
A fire occurred on Wednesday morning at
the extensive spinning mill -belonging to
Thomas Barnes and Co., Farnworth. After
raging about three hours the fire was subdued.
The damage is said to be about £5,000.
A serious accident occurred on Wednesday
at the works of the Chillington Company, in
Wolverhampton, b' the explosion .pf one of a
range of firing boilers. The scalding water
and steam were scattered about the rolling
mills, and a man and three boys were badly
scalded. A lad named Manning is so severely
hurt that his life is despaired of. The cause of
the explosion has not yet been ascertained.
It is stated that the boiler was well supplied
with water, and all the boilers at the works are
insured, and regularly inspected, The acci-
dent poured at a time when most of the hand*
had left for breakfast.

articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

On Saturday the Old Catholics at Cologne
brought their three day's Congress to a most
satisfactory close. Important resolutions have
been arrived at, not only for the Catholic
Church of Germany, but for Christendom at
large. A scheme of organization has been
devised, founded on a union of the episcopal
and synodal principles. A declaration has
been made in favour of compulsory civil
marriage with civil registration. At the last
sitting a commission was appointed to promote
communion with other churches and confes-
sions, and to facilitate the reconciliation of
prevailing differences of belief. The public
meeting which followed the conferences was
attended by three thousand persons, including
many ladies.

Another Republican anniversary has passed
over in France without any demonstration to
embarrass the Government. M. Gambetta, in
•presiding at a private banquet at St. Etienne,
defined Republican equality as being founded
on the rights and labour of all, adding a
significant qualification that there were enlight-
ened men whose mission it was to guide and
instruot their fellows. On being summoned to
harangue a crowd outside the banquet-room,
he conjured the mothers present to bring up
their children as avengers of their country.
A monster banquet at Chambery, for which a
thousand persons had aubscribea, was peremp-
torily forbidden by the authorities.

Speedy work has been made of M. About at
the Strasburg court-martial, On the recom-
mendation of the Judge-Advocate he was
acquitted, and allowed to leave the town,
which he did forthwith. He has telegraphed
to his friends in Paris that the Imperial
prosecutor had determined to give the Paris
press a lesson through him, but was foiled by
the Judge-Advocate. Characteristically, he
concluded by saying that he had "much to
tell."

M. Casimir Perier's approximation to the
Conservative Republic is progressing. He is
expected soon to supersede M. Lefan.c at the
Home Office. As a further blow to the
Orleanist cause, the Duke of Aumale's de-
claration that, though favourable to Con-
stitutional Monarchy, he would bow to tho
national will; has been reproduced by the
Parisian papers.

An important and ominous change is an-
nounced as about to take place at the German
Embassy in Paris. Count von Arnim has
requested leave to resign, and, in the event of
his doing so, the Imperial Chancellor, it is
said, does not intend to appoint a successor.
The embassy would be temporarily reduced to
a consulate. This statement of the Echo de
Parlemorit hardly accords with a telegram
from Berlin, that the Count has been created
a Privy Councillor, with the title of Excel-
lency.

Princess Bismarck and her son, who were
stated to have arrived at Torquay, are still at
Varzin.

King L onis of Bavaria 'appears to have re-
linqUished his Quixotic design of sottingp a
particularist anti-Imperial Ministry. Herr
Pfretsohner, the present Minister of Finance,
has had the portfolio of Foreign Affairs pressed
upon him, and the latest rumour in Munich is
that he had accepted it. If so the crisis will
have ended in a mere shuffling of the cards,
without much change of policy.

Berne has celebrated the anniversary of its
emancipation with a joy unmarred by any poll.
tidal disturbance, but somewhat damped, by
unfavourable weather.

Oscar 11., of Sweden, brother of the late
King and Prince Regent, has been proclaimed
at Stockholm, and taken the oath of allegiance
to the Constitution. King Charles's remains
arc to be embalmed at Malmo prior to removal
to the capital for interment. In the proclama-
tion announcing his accession the new King
says that his motto will be "The welfare of
both peoples."

"Permanent financial equilibrium" is one
of the secondary merits prognosticated of the
forthcoming Spanish Budget. It has been
approved by the Government, and has been
submitted to the Cortes.

Bona-fide travellers have scored a victory
over the Licensing Act at Highgate-hill. Two
publieans from that quarter, who were charged
at Clerkenwell Police-court with serving
customers at illegal hours on Sunday, have
escaped on the plea that they had asked each
man if he was a bona-fide traveller. The magis-
trate ruled this to be a sufficient observation
of the Act. A grand combination of the trade
in the Isle of Wight has had a successful
effeet upon the magistrates in obtaining from
them an extension of the time of closing to
twelve o'clock. The same indulgence, though
urgently demandedt ha Won refused at
Rugby.

William Webb, of Frome, died recently at
the extraordinary age of 105. The deceased,
who received his discharge from the Royal
Marines in 1799, was confined to his bed for
only a short period, and had walked out within
the past two months.

His Royal Highness Prince Leopold will, it
is stated, commence a course of study at Ox-
ford in October term. It is also reported that
Prince Ii assan's younger brothers will shortly
enter at Oxford.

On Saturday Mr. J. Payne held an inquest
at the City of London Union, Thavies-inn, oh
the body of Joseph Clark, aged 63. The
evidence of deceased's, eldest daughter and a
younger sister proved that he had often
threatened to destroy himself unless his work
got better. After Thursday night nothing
was seen of him until about a quarter before
seven o'clock the following morning, when his
body was found by a lighterman floating down
the river,, off the City Gasworks,. The jury
returned a verdict of Temporary Insanity.

A new planet of small dimensions and
belonging to the group of asteroids situated
between Mars and Jupiter, was discovered at
the Paris Observatory on the night of the 11th
by M. Prosper Henry, assistant astronomer.

The Prince and. Princess of Wales on Mon-
day left Blair Athol° for Abergeldie Castle.
The weather was cold, a good deal of snow
having fallen.

The September sessions of the Central Crimi-
nal Court were opened on Monday, when
there were GO prisoners for trial. 'William
Luke, who had been indicted for stealing
several hundred pounds, the propeity of his
employers, was acquitted. Solomon
.Davis
was convicted of perjury, and sentenced to
twelve months' imprisonment. In a similar
charge against a man named Pollock a verdict
of not guilty was returned.

A cab driver who had assaulted three
policemen has been sent to prison for six

A party of visitors to Scarborough have had
a narrow escape from being drowned. Whilst
attempting to walk along the beach from Scar-

tide in a bay formed by projecting cliffs. For
several hours their only place of safety was a
narrow ledge of rock, and it was only by the
promptness of the Scarborough coastguards-
men that they were rescued from their
dangerous position.

A farm-labourer, while returning to his
work on a farm in the neighbourhood of Ayr,
on Saturday morning, found a man lying by
the roadside in a dying state, with a deep
wound in his breast. Before he could tell the
circumstances of the attack made on him, the
unfortunate man expired; and all that is
known is that he was an engineer belonging
to Glasgow, who had been attending Ayr
races. The authorities are investigating the
affair, which is as yet involved in mystery,
the name even of the murdered man being
unknown.

Several private dinners took place in Paris
on Sunday to celebrate the anniversary of the
proclamation of the First Republic, the
Government having objected to the public
banquet proposed, to which 160 guests had
been invited. At one of these dinners the
company was somewhat numerous. M. Victor
Hugo and M. Louis Blanc, who had been
invited, sent letters of excuse on the ground
of their absence from France. The latter said
that he was in favour of celebrating anniver-
saries which recalled the triumph of right.
He was of opinion that the First Empire, the
Restoration, the Government of July, and the
Second Empire were mere interludes, and
that the spirit of the nation was persistently
Republican. M. 'Victor Hugo in a charac-
teristic letter referred to Liberty, Equality,
and Fraternity as the three powers which
were certain to vanquish the there European
Empires.

rOVBRTY, CRIME, AND EMIGRA-
TION.

To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

Sin,—The rental of lands at present unap-
propriated in Australia, in Canada, and in
many other portions of the world, could surely
at no distant date be easily made to support
fully the pauperism of this country, no other
fund being at all necessary for that pur-
pose.
In Australia, km , however, we are selling—
nay, even giving away—the land as fast as we
can, neither receiving, nor attempting to re-
ceive anything in exchange for it. Thus,
while at home we are loud clamourers for a
general nationalization of the laud, even at an
immense cost, and in oppposition to vested
interests on all hands, in Australia, &e., with
:not an atom of profit to ourselves, our obvious
spolicy, on the contrary., is positively the utter
de-nationalization of the laved;
Again, at home or abroad, we are found
,with remarkable discrimination, and with a
special eye to efficiency, to organize sections
of our poor and others for 'purposes of mere
bloodshed and murder—holding Men, officers,
colleges, die., all in beautiful array at any
time for the destruction of ivealth, and the
universal spread of misery; but no one, either
at home or abroad, , seems to dream of our
forming an army of industry, as duly
be-officered and be-colleged also, out of these
same paupers or other volunteers; and yet an
twiny of thio iatter kiwi Would aerie our

interests far better, be far less eo'stly, and,
moreover, would widely extend the blessings
of biviliiation and pOaco all over the
world.
Now, such an army as this lad proposed,
with depots in many directions in the mother

country,- might on-all sides collect for the
foreign service of our national industry (and
on similar principles, too) material suited to
its purpose.
These, then setting out under due subor-
dination for Australia, tor Africa; for America,
or for any or every other part of the globe (lieing
primarily supported by Governmental ad-
vances), large tracts of country could soon be
opened for civilised and civilising purposes;
and care in meantime being taken to render
every member of such an army in every
desirable sense as fit as possible for his posi-
tion, selectidns could now be made from the
best prepared, and to these, either individually
or collectively, at a moderate rental frdm the
State (i.e., at a tax proportioned to the general
expenses)—land, seed, implements, &0., could
be adequately supplied—the competent and
worthy thus soon securing for themselves
independence; the incompetent or the un-
worthy dono feniaining under the original
jurisdiction for additional itistruotion, &0.,
&c.

In a similar way criminal colonics (islands
being most desirable for the purpose) could be
distinctly formed and conducted—with this
exception only, that the convict should never
be allowed to leave his colony, or again to
corhniunicate with the world which once pub-
licly banished hiut----grades cif punishment
being marked by districts, and districts by
different degrees and hours of work, and by
variations of diet, liberty, ite.
The above, then, sufficing in illustration of
the principle for which I am contending;
details I do not at present even attempt to
deal With If, however, 1 have adequately
shown that by the means proposed poverty
and crime may be fairly and judiciously en-
countered, and made, as it were, self-support=
ing, with full relief to the mother country,
my purpose for the time is also adequately
servedi

For the test, I have only to say that all
expenses; direct or indiregt, in connection with
either the industrial or the criminal colony
proposed, should be borne, either as a debt or
otherwise, respectively by those colonies; and
that charges fot rent and the apportionment
of the hours of labour in either should also
respectively be modified by the amount of
those direct or indirect expenses.
As to complaints from tradesmen and others,
of the injury done to trade, dte., by the work
either of paupers of criminals, it may only be
necessary to point out that, had the men whose
work is, or might be complained of, been
neither paupers nor criminals; their work for
themselves Could not have been stopped; and
that, therefore, as paupers or criminals, their
work for the benefit of the State or society as
a whole oould not fairly be objected to.
Further, if from tenderness to the inte.
rests of certain tradesmen, cte., paupers or
criminals are to oe maintained in idleness,
then all the rest of society would have to be
taxed in the interest of those few tradesmen,
&c., which, from the foregoing consideration,
would certainly be absurd in the extreme.
In conclusion, I have merely .to add that,
had the principle I am now contending for
been publicly adopted in by-gone days, that
is, had colonial lands then, and thenceforward,
been let only, instead of being sold, very
different issues haply would in many ways
have characterized for us the present time.
However, as it is never, perhaps, too late for
us, even nationally, either to learn or to
amend, it might be well for us, as soon as
possible, publicly to determine the value of
the following propositions:-
1. That Government dispose of no more
colonial lands in any quarter of the globe.
2. That Government, on the contrary, in all
possible directions, wherever cheapness or
other circumstance recommends, buy up all
available lands in the market.

8. That Government do not for the present
make any purchases of home-lands, which
must necessarily be dear lands.
4. That existing holders of home-lands,
empowered by law at any time to devise their
Property at will, or to dispose of the same to
direct successors, be publicly recommended .to
let their estates in perpetuity (subject only to
a due payment of a fixed amount of rental,
to themselves or their successors), to co-
operative bodies of men rather than to indi-
viduals.—l am, Sir, yours, &c

- W.A, RUSSELL.

THE WAY TO RAISE WAGES.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
81)4—Yesterday at the meeting of the Social
Science Congress, Sir John Bowring, in his
address on "The Value of Statistics," touched
upon the recent increase in prioe of all the
necessities of life, and said that this would fall
the heaviest on the opulent of the middle
classes and the agricultural labourers. He
showed that workmen employed in manufac-
tories had by combination raised the rate of
wages and decreased the hours of work. This
is what the agricultural lAbourorp 000 k to do,

It is very. pleasant to hear that to help them a
little the Society of Boilermakers and Iron
Shipbuilders hate made a levy, and have been
able to assist them to the amount of nearly
£l7O. Now, Ido not believe the Society
wishes in any way to encourage strikes among
them, but simply to aid those to whom union is
strength. They deserve as much as any to
participate in the improved state of things
among the working classes, and there will be
many glad to know they are getting a helping
hand from those who are in a better position
than themselves. But, it behoves all interested
—both employers and employed—to take the
advice giveri by Sir John to the first, that "they
should cede the reasonable demands of their
servants"; and the latter that "they should
carefully guard their savings in the day of
prosperity, as the day of adversity would
assuredly come.' —I am, &0.,
Liverpool, Sept. 18th, 1872.

STANDING ARMIES AND THE
WORKING CLASSES.
To the Editor of the BEz-lirn.
Sin,—l noticed in your correspondence of
Saturday last a letter on the above question,
signed W. Bruce. As lam rather in favour
of the opinion held by Mr. Latham, I should
like to say a few words on the subject.
Mr. Bruce, in his letter/ aoknowledges that
"standing armies" are a disgrace te civili-
zation ;" he also says, "it is one of the most
painful and disheartening thoughts to the
lover of humanity and progress, that we are
now in possession of weapons of war calculated
to kill mare men in a shorter time than in
any previous period of the world's history, and
feel quite certain that most persons will
agree that it is a pity that so many able-bodied
men are trained up for the special purpose of
killing each other." Yes, Mr. Editor, I not
only think it is a pity, but I think it is a
shame that such a thing should be tolerated
in this Christian England of ours. The state-
ment is made that the masses arc not alive to
their interests fr if this is so, it is high time
they were aveaksned to think and act for
themselves, but I think they are gradually
coming to see the monstrous injustice which
they are compelled to bear under the standing
army system.
lie eliarges the "peace party" with being
"one-sided," but is it not rather on the side of
those, who think that "standing armies" are
a great evil (as he does not deny), but yet
think that we' ought to keep them up, simply,
because, as they think, that England's " sun "
Will set for over, an the day that we abolish
our army. If England's "sun" sets, because
we abolish what is a source of misery., and a
great evil to the country, then, all I say is,
let It set, for sooner would I see it sat, than
that we should allow such a monstrous in-
justice to continue in our land.
The " Ifritish lion" only, he says, "keeps
other monarchies from encroaching upon our
property and possessions." I rather think Mr.
Brace has not had his pen under complete
control when he wrote this high-sounding
compliment, for if either Russia or Prussia, or
any other great warlike nation, were to declare
war against the "British lion," I should
tremble for the consequences. I should say,
the power of the "British lion" lies not in
her army (as Mr. Bruce would have us believe),
but rather in her character as a nation; as a
natidn she is well-known as one who will give
justice where justice is due, and will have
justice done to her, and that without having
recourse to the curse of civilization, "stand-
ing armies."
Our army," he says, "is aneeessity, adread-
ful necessity, a deplorable necessity, but it is a
necessity.' What a startling thing, if true; is
it necessary that we should train and keep
men for the solo purpose of fighting, or are
they only' kept for the purpose of gratifying
the ambition of the upper classes of society?
for it is well-known that in the greater part
of the wars in which England has been
engaged we have been urged to it by those
very people who turn pale at the thought of
our being without an army.
His argument on the "police forces" looks
good on the surface, but to examine it closely
will show that it is only a bugbear, for the
" police " are employed to bring men to
justice who have broken the laws of the
country; but, on the other hand, "armies "are
only kept, something similar to men keeping
bull dogs, to let loose at one another on the
slightest possible pretext. But, thanks to the
progress of Christianity, we have, 1 hope,
found a way in which we can settle questions '
of great importance without our national bull-
dogs, I mean the "Court of Arbitration." Who
can deny that ten years ago we should net
have rushed headlong to war with America
on the " Alabama " question?
But I must conclude, as I fear I am taking
too much of your valuable space. I have not ,
done full justice to the subject, owing to the
short time which I have had. at my disposal.
Hoping you will pardon me, Mr. Editor, for
trespassing on your space.--Yours,
3. B. REDruas.
