To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

Sra,—My letter on this subject, which yea
were goad enough to insert in your issue Otto
14th mat, seems, if 1 may judge from the
expressions made use of by 11r. Latham, and,
also, Mr. Campin, to have somewhat puzzled
, some of your readers. Perhaps you will per 4
mit me to give a short explanation of inY
argument,
First, however, a word with Mr. Latham.
had no intention in using the phrase " closet:
spun theories "to "upset "that gentleman. II
I could see that have given him cause to be
angry, I would at once express regret fir
having used the phrase, But as I did not,
and do not, rook upon him as the originator
of, or in any way responsible for, the well Worn
and rather commonplace assumption—it closet-
spun theories "—on which his "Boot Ques-
tions " are based, I see no reason for doing
so.

In replying to both gentlemen, I may oer
that I did not assert, to use Mr. 'Athol)] e
words, that I would "seek to benefit the nation
by greatly increasing the number of men in the
army, and adding as much as possible to their
pay.' Nor, in those of Mr. Campin, " that
the money spent in keeping men at work oa
unproductive industry is any good to the
nation." What I argued was that the dig'
missal of the army, as proposed by Mr. Latham,
would inflict a cruel injury upon the operative
classes. What effect it would have upon the
nation is quite a separate question, and I
should advise Mr. Latham, if he ever bore to
be logical, not to confound questions which ato
not the same.

I am quite justified in making a distinction
between what is profitable to the nation, and
what is advantageous to but a section of it,
It is a distinction eonstantly made by the poli-
tical economists, that what is taken from one por-
tion of a nation and given to another, is merely
taking from Peter and giving to Paul, and is
not necessarily injurious to the national
wealth. What one loses another gains.
Nothing which either of your correspondents
has said has touched the question whether
Mr. Latham'sproposal would, or would not, be
injurious to the working classes? Perhaps
nothing of smaller interest than the welfare of
the nation at large engages their attention.
Yet one would imagine that the questions,
whether it would be advantageous to the
working classes to throw upon the labour
market the 80,000 soldiers and the 160,000
workers who are now supported by supplying
the requirements of the army, might demand
a more thoughtful consideration than is neces-
sary to shape a flippant phrase.
Let us see what encouragement political
economy holds out to induce working men SD
make a "Root Question" of a plan for over-
crowding the labour market. It gives him,
under such circumstances, a choice of two
things. .1. Emigration when, perhaps he has
not a shilling in his pockets. 2. That in-
evitable thinning Of his ranks by grim death,
which hard times, aided by fever, want, and
diseases of all kinds, so rapidly achieves. DO
either of these alternatives offer the working
man a prospect about which he is likely to
become enthusiastic? - At- a time, too, of all
others, when, by great saerifices, he seems to
have almost grasped the control of the labour
market by the reductions he has obtained in
the length of his working day.

I am by no means opposed to International
Arbitration; I wish it every success. But Mr.
Latham writes as if the disbanding of armies.
must precede the adoption of an International
Tribunal. That is simply putting the cart
before the horse, mistaking cause for effect.
Armies will never be abolished to make vitt)"
for a Court of International Appeal. That
eourt will have, gradually and tentatively, to
establish itself, and as the nations gain confi-
dence in it they will lean upon it instead of
upon armed millions. In that way, slowly,
but I hope surely, armies will disappear.
Their abolition will be a consequence flowing
from arbitration, if ever it becomes generally
adopted, not producing it.
WILLIAM H. LAIRD.

An inquest was held on Wednesday at
Sheffield on the body of an old man named
William Cooney. Deceased was found on
Monday night in an insensible condition in
Russell-street, Sheffield, by a police-officer,
who looked him up in the station on a charge
of drunkenness. At half-past three o'clock
next morning Cooney was found dead in the
cell. A post-mortem examination showed
that deceased's skull was fractured in two
places. The investigation was adjourned for
n. week. Inquiries have led to a suspicion of
foul play.
